P0E47.description: P0E47 means pack voltage measurement E reports more voltage than the pack can reach even when fully charged. A sense lead touching a higher potential, a broken divider resistor or a damaged input of the measuring chip are the usual explanations; real overcharging is unlikely when only one channel shows it. P0E47 is not documented by any manufacturer in public. The 2013 GM two-mode hybrid pickups and SUVs test the analogous channel A against 430 V (P0ABD), using the same 300-of-400 counter at 10 ms and running the test only while the 12 V network sits between 9 and 18 V. CARB requires battery voltage sensors to be tested against plausible limits. Low and plausibility faults of channel E are P0E46 and P0E45. Expect a warning and restricted electric drive.

causes.label: Sense lead of channel E chafed through and touching a higher potential
Broken divider resistor or lost reference in the measuring circuit
Damaged measuring input or software fault in the battery controller

symptoms: MIL and hybrid warning on
Charging or regenerative braking restricted
Electric drive limited or blocked

P0E48.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E48.description: P0E48 marks pack voltage measurement E as unsteady: the signal jumps, drops out for fractions of a second or changes faster than a battery voltage can, and then returns to normal. Because the fault comes and goes, it is often found only as a stored code after a brief warning. No manufacturer documents P0E48 publicly, and GM's published hybrid tables, for example those of the 2013 two-mode trucks, test pack voltage only for low, high and rationality faults on channel A. CARB requires circuit monitoring of battery voltage sensors in the energy storage system. Steady faults of the same channel are P0E44 to P0E47; channel F uses P0E4D for this fault type. Loose or corroded sense terminals and chafed leads that react to vibration or heat are the usual suspects.

causes.label: Loose, pushed-back or corroded terminal on the channel E sense lead
Chafed sense lead that shorts briefly under vibration
Intermittent fault in the battery controller input

symptoms: Warning light that comes and goes
Brief losses of electric power, often on rough roads
Stored code without a current fault

P0E49.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit
P0E49.description: Channel F is the sixth and last pack voltage measurement in this series and comes after channel E (P0E44 to P0E48). P0E49 is its general circuit fault: the battery controller cannot use the input, for instance because the sense line is open, the measuring chip reports an internal error or the raw value is missing, while no clear low, high or erratic pattern applies. No manufacturer documents P0E49 publicly. Systems that compare several high-voltage measurements, as GM's 2019 hybrids do between the pack sensor and the inverter and charger bus voltages, depend on every channel being valid. CARB requires all battery voltage sensors of the storage system to be monitored. The vehicle typically limits or refuses high-voltage operation.

causes.label: Open sense lead or disconnected connector of channel F
Internal fault of the voltage measuring chip or battery controller
Moisture or corrosion in the pack-side connector

symptoms: High-voltage warning and reduced power
Vehicle may refuse to become ready

P0E4A.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit Range/Performance
P0E4A.description: P0E4A reports that pack voltage measurement F lies within its electrical range but disagrees with a reference value. No manufacturer documents P0E4A publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables show two plausibility checks such a channel could face: P0ABB fails when pack voltage and the summed cell voltages differ by more than 12 V in 20 of 25 samples at 25 ms, and P0AF8 compares the pack sensor with the inverter bus voltage, failing at more than 13.95 V difference in 400 of 500 samples, or at more than 14.95 V against the charger bus. Both are Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. CARB requires rationality monitoring of battery voltage sensors. The electrical faults of channel F are P0E49, P0E4B and P0E4C; channel E uses P0E45.

causes.label: Contact resistance at a sense terminal distorting the channel F value
Fault in the comparison value, such as the inverter bus or cell voltage measurement
Measuring drift or software issue in the battery controller

symptoms: MIL on in the first trip with reduced battery power
Implausible state of charge display

P0E4B.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit Low
P0E4B.description: P0E4B sets when pack voltage measurement F falls below its plausible minimum, which normally points to a sense path shorted to ground, an open sense fuse or a defective input of the battery controller. No manufacturer documents P0E4B publicly. As a reference, the battery energy control module in GM's 2019 hybrid tables sets the channel A code P0ABC when pack-side voltage stays under 24 V for 1.6 s within a 2 s window, Type A, one trip, as long as system voltage is at least 9 V. CARB requires out-of-range checks of battery voltage sensors. P0E4C is the high counterpart, P0E4A the plausibility fault, and the matching low code of channel E is P0E46. Because precharge and contactor checks rely on the reading, the vehicle may not reach ready mode.

causes.label: Channel F sense lead shorted to ground or pack housing
Open fuse or resistor in the channel F sense path
Failed analog input of the battery controller

symptoms: No ready mode or contactors do not close
MIL and high-voltage warning on

P0E4C.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit High
P0E4C.description: P0E4C means pack voltage measurement F reports a value above anything the battery can produce. Common reasons are a sense line in contact with a higher potential, a lost ground reference in the measuring circuit or a faulty analog input, so the channel rather than the cells is suspect. No manufacturer documents P0E4C publicly. In GM's 2019 hybrid tables the channel A code P0ABD sets above 479 V, again 1.6 s within 2 s and Type A. CARB requires battery voltage sensors to be checked against upper and lower limits. Real overvoltage of single cells is reported by cell voltage codes such as P0DE7, while the low fault of channel F is P0E4B and the same high fault on channel E is P0E47. The controller usually blocks or limits electric operation.

causes.label: Channel F sense line touching a higher potential
Lost ground reference or broken divider in the measuring circuit
Faulty analog input or software of the battery controller

symptoms: Warning lamp and limited electric drive
Charging interrupted or not started

P0E4D.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E4D.description: P0E4D flags pack voltage measurement F as intermittent: short dropouts, spikes or steps that a real high-voltage battery cannot make, followed by normal readings again. Where a vehicle cross-checks several voltage sensors, as GM does in its 2019 hybrids between the pack sensor and the inverter or charger bus (P0AF8), such glitches can also surface as correlation faults. No manufacturer documents P0E4D publicly. Under CARB rules the storage system's voltage sensors must be watched for circuit faults. Permanent faults of channel F are P0E49 to P0E4C, the same fault type on channel E is P0E48. Typical triggers are loose sense terminals, corrosion inside connectors and leads that move with vibration, so the symptoms appear and vanish.

causes.label: Loose or corroded terminal in the channel F sense circuit
Sense lead that loses contact when the harness moves
Interference or intermittent fault in the measuring electronics

symptoms: Intermittent warning light
Sporadic power limitation
Additional correlation codes stored

P0E4E.title: Engine Failed to Crank
P0E4E.description: P0E4E reports that the hybrid system commanded an engine start but the crankshaft did not turn, or did not reach the cranking speed it expected. It differs from P0A0F, where the engine is turned over but does not fire and keep running. In most hybrids a motor-generator fed by the high-voltage battery cranks the engine, so causes range from a seized engine or transaxle to missing battery energy or a drive fault. No manufacturer documents P0E4E publicly. GM's bulletin PIC6229C for the 2016-2019 Malibu hybrid shows why charge matters: below a pack voltage of 154 to 210 V, depending on temperature, the system stops trying to crank until a recovery charge is done. CARB requires the energy storage monitor to catch faults that prevent engine starts.

causes.label: High-voltage battery too low to crank, often after repeated failed starts
Mechanically seized engine or blocked transaxle
Fault in the cranking motor-generator, its inverter or a conventional starter
Crankshaft speed not detected because of a sensor or signal fault

symptoms: Engine does not turn over when the hybrid system calls for it
Vehicle runs electrically only or shows a stop-safely warning
No start at all once the battery is depleted

P0E4F.title: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E4F.description: P0E4F covers coolant pump A of the motor electronics loop, which cools the inverter and drive motor, and sets when the signal exchanged with the pump becomes unstable rather than permanently open or shorted. Ford uses exactly this code in the OBD summaries for its hybrid and plug-in hybrid models of 2015 to 2019: the pump reports back to the module, and P0E4F is stored when that feedback is outside the expected frequency or duty cycle for more than 1 s. The check runs continuously from 500 ms after power-up with 6 to 19 V on the 12 V network, next to P0A05 (no response for over 9.25 s), P0A06 and P0A07 (driver faults) and P0C73 (pump reports an internal fault). Loose pins or moisture in the pump connector are typical; overheat protection may cut power.

causes.label: Loose, corroded or wet pins in the pump A connector
Chafed command or feedback wire that loses contact intermittently
Failing electronics inside the pump sending an unstable feedback signal
Unstable 12 V supply or poor ground at the pump

symptoms: MIL or hybrid system warning
Power reduction when inverter or motor temperature rises
Fault may clear itself and return later

P0E50.title: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E50.description: P0E50 is the intermittent or erratic fault of the control circuit for coolant pump B, the second electric pump some hybrids use in the inverter and motor electronics cooling. No manufacturer documents P0E50 publicly. The closest published example is Ford's pump A version, P0E4F, stored when the pump's feedback leaves its expected frequency or duty cycle for over 1 s. Second pumps of this kind are in service: on the 2024 Jeep Compass 4xe, Stellantis bulletin 08-200-24 cures the pump B performance code P0C74 by reprogramming the hybrid control processors. CARB requires inverter cooling outputs to be monitored for circuit faults. Steady open, low and high faults of pump B are P0B38 to P0B3A. Short dropouts briefly reduce coolant flow and may trigger a power limit.

causes.label: Intermittent contact at the pump B connector or a harness splice
Pump B electronics producing an unstable signal
Control module software evaluating the pump signal too strictly

symptoms: Warning light that appears now and then
Temporary power reduction under high load or heat

P0E51.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit
P0E51.description: P0E51 is the general circuit fault of current sensor A in a DC/DC converter, the element that tells the converter's controller how many amps flow through its power stage. The code covers a signal path that is broken in a way the controller cannot sort into low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0E51 publicly. The same sensor appears in Mercedes-Benz information LI54.10-P-079533 for the EQB and G-Class, where a short to positive is stored as P0E5400. Ford's hybrid summaries show what such a check looks at: at power-up the inductor current sensor of the boost converter must show less than 15 A offset and a raw signal between 4.5 and 6.0 V, though Ford files these faults under P0A11. CARB requires circuit checks on hybrid input components. Converter output is usually limited.

causes.label: Current sensor inside the converter defective (usually not replaceable separately)
Loose, corroded or damaged sensor connection or harness
Fault on the converter control board or its sensor supply
Converter or hybrid control software needs an update

symptoms: Hybrid or 12 V battery warning in the instrument cluster
12 V battery is charged poorly or not at all
Reduced electric power or limited hybrid functions

P0E52.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0E52.description: P0E52 is the plausibility test of current sensor A: the signal is electrically valid, yet the measured current does not fit what the converter is doing. Two makers name it. FCA lists it for the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid; bulletin 08-037-21 brings new HCP software and turns P0E52 from a two-trip into a one-trip code, so the MIL may light after a single faulty drive. Ford reports it from the inverter system controller of the 2024–2026 Lincoln Nautilus and the 2025–2026 Maverick hybrid, together with several motor and inverter codes; the car loses power and shows Stop Safely Now or Service Vehicle Soon, and the special service message tells dealers to replace that controller. Pure circuit faults are P0E51, P0E53 and P0E54.

causes.label: Control software with unsuitable limits (FCA eTorque HCP update)
Internal fault of the inverter system controller (Ford hybrid)
Current sensor drifting or offset out of tolerance
High resistance at sensor connector or ground

symptoms: MIL on, often after only one drive
Limited power with Stop Safely Now or Service Vehicle Soon message
Reduced eTorque assist or start/stop function

P0E53.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit Low
P0E53.description: P0E53 means the signal of DC/DC converter current sensor A sits below its valid window. On a Hall-type sensor with a mid-scale zero point, that usually points to a short to ground, a missing sensor supply or an open signal wire pulled low, not to a real drop in current. No manufacturer documents P0E53 publicly. Ford's hybrid summaries show the kind of window involved: the boost stage's inductor current signal counts as valid only from 4.5 to 6.0 V, so a lower raw value is a fault, although Ford stores it under the collective code P0A11. Mercedes-Benz reports the opposite fault of the same sensor on the EQB and G-Class as P0E5400. CARB demands out-of-range checks on such inputs. With no usable current reading the converter is normally throttled or shut down.

causes.label: Signal line shorted to ground
Sensor supply missing or too low
Current sensor or converter electronics defective

symptoms: Hybrid or charging-system warning lamp
12 V battery discharges because the converter does not supply it
Reduced power or electric drive not available

P0E54.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit High
P0E54.description: P0E54 reports a current sensor A signal above the range the DC/DC converter accepts. Mercedes-Benz uses it explicitly: its bulletin LI54.10-P-079533, covering the EQB (series 243) and the G-Class including the electric G 580 (series 465), defines P0E5400 as a short to positive of the converter's current sensor A. It is one of up to four converter codes, with P0C3B00, P0E9700 and P0C4000, that appear after the converter wakes up incorrectly; drivers see a red 12 V battery message and HV warnings. Mercedes treats it as a state error rather than a broken part: the technician runs the buck mode in XENTRY for about 30 s, checks that output current settles from a high initial value, then clears the memory or resets the converter. The low-signal sibling is P0E53.

causes.label: Converter stuck in a fault state after incorrect wake-up (Mercedes 243/465)
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Current sensor or converter electronics defective

symptoms: Red 12 V battery message
White or yellow high-voltage system warnings
Reduced drive power

P0E55.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E55.description: P0E55 deals with a current sensor A reading that flickers or vanishes for moments instead of failing for good. FCA documents it repeatedly for the Ram 1500 with eTorque mild hybrid, where the DC/DC converter sits in the 48 V battery pack and is run by the battery pack control module (BPCM). Bulletin 08-030-24 for the 2019 model lists P0E55 among ten BPCM codes; 08-333-25 and its revision 08-283-26 for the 2025 truck with the 3.6 litre V6 name it alone and describe the result: the 12 V battery is not kept charged, runs flat soon after driving and may leave the truck needing a tow, later also with limp-home mode and disabled start/stop. In all cases the fix is new BPCM software, not a part. Steady circuit faults are P0E51, P0E53 and P0E54.

causes.label: Battery pack control module software (FCA eTorque, reflash)
Loose or corroded contact in the sensor path
Current sensor or converter electronics failing intermittently

symptoms: MIL on
12 V battery not charging, flat soon after driving
Limp-home mode and start/stop disabled

P0E56.title: DC/DC Converter Input Voltage Too Low
P0E56.description: P0E56 says the voltage arriving at the input of the DC/DC converter, normally the high-voltage bus of the traction battery, is lower than the converter needs to work. Unlike the sensor codes, the reading itself is believed; the supply is the problem. No manufacturer documents P0E56 on an official public server. Converter makers build in the matching guard: Poclain's 48 V unit runs from 36 V upward and switches off by undervoltage lockout near 28 V, restarting only around 30 V. Ford's hybrid summaries apply a similar floor to the inverter input under a different code, P1A07, below 150 V for 100 ms. CARB requires hybrid components to be monitored. Causes range from a deeply discharged or disconnected battery to open contactors or a fault in the HV cabling; the 12 V system then loses its charge source.

causes.label: Traction battery deeply discharged or limited by its management system
Main contactor not closing or high-voltage cable/connector fault
Input voltage measurement inside the converter faulty

symptoms: 12 V battery warning, battery discharges while driving
Hybrid system warning, vehicle may not reach ready mode
Reduced power

P0E57.title: DC/DC Converter Input Voltage Too High
P0E57.description: P0E57 is set when the DC/DC converter sees more voltage on its input than it is rated for. Excess input voltage stresses the switching transistors and input capacitors, so a converter typically stops working to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P0E57 on an official public server. Supplier data show the limits involved: Poclain specifies 96 V as the highest continuous input for its 48 V converter. Ford's hybrid summaries treat a comparable overvoltage on the inverter side as P0C79, triggered when the DC bus measurement exceeds 516 V for 10 ms. CARB requires such hybrid components to be monitored. Typical triggers are a boost stage regulating too high, a charging or regenerative event without proper voltage control, or a faulty voltage measurement. The 12 V supply may stop while the code is active.

causes.label: High-voltage bus driven too high by boost stage, regeneration or charging
Input voltage measurement in the converter reads too high
Hybrid or battery control software needs an update

symptoms: Hybrid system or 12 V battery warning
Converter switches off temporarily, 12 V voltage drops
Reduced power or limited regeneration

P0E58.title: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P0E58.description: P0E58 stands for a general circuit fault of the third temperature sensor in a DC/DC converter, after sensors A (P0C38 ff.) and B (P0C3D ff.). Which part of the converter sensor C watches is up to the maker. At Ford it is the inductor of the variable voltage converter, the boost stage of its full hybrids, but Ford uses only the plausibility code P0E59 for it. No manufacturer documents P0E58 publicly. The code is meant for a fault the controller can detect without being able to classify it as too low, too high or implausible, for example an unstable reference or supply. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid input components. Without this reading the controller protects the converter by limiting its power, which can cut electric assist.

causes.label: Sensor connection or wiring damaged or corroded
Temperature sensor in the converter defective
Sensor reference or evaluation circuit in the converter faulty

symptoms: Hybrid system warning
Reduced electric assist or power

P0E59.title: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0E59.description: P0E59 is the best-documented member of this group. Ford's hybrid OBD summaries from 2015 to 2019 assign it to the inductor temperature sensor of the variable voltage converter and monitor it without pause once 500 ms have passed since power-up, provided the 12 V supply lies between 6 and 19 V. It fails on any of three conditions: a sensor voltage under 0.067 V or over 4.86 V, an inductor reading above 165 °C for 1 s, or a value more than 30 °C away from engine coolant temperature after a soak of 180 minutes. Ford thus folds the electrical range checks into this code instead of using P0E5A/P0E5B. FCA also uses P0E59 on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque; bulletin 08-037-21 makes it a one-trip code with new HCP software. Sensors A and B have P0C39 and P0C3E as their plausibility codes.

causes.label: Inductor temperature sensor drifting, reading off after cold soak
Inductor really overheating, e.g. due to weak electronics cooling
Hybrid control software (FCA HCP update)
Short or open in the sensor circuit (Ford range limits)

symptoms: MIL on, at FCA after one faulty drive
Reduced hybrid assist or electric driving
Hybrid system warning

P0E5A.title: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P0E5A.description: P0E5A means the voltage from DC/DC converter temperature sensor C has fallen below its valid window. With the NTC thermistors common in power electronics, a low voltage translates into an implausibly hot reading, so a grounded signal wire or a failed sensor is far more likely than genuine overheating. No manufacturer documents P0E5A publicly. Ford gives an idea of the window for its sensor C, the inductor sensor of the boost converter: anything under 0.067 V counts as a fault, but Ford stores it as P0E59, not as P0E5A. CARB requires out-of-range monitoring of hybrid input components. Because the controller must assume overtemperature, it usually derates the converter at once, which can reduce electric power. The high-signal counterpart is P0E5B.

causes.label: Sensor signal shorted to ground
Thermistor internally shorted
Evaluation circuit in the converter faulty

symptoms: Hybrid system warning
Converter derated, reduced electric power

P0E5B.title: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P0E5B.description: P0E5B is stored when the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor C rises above its valid window. On an NTC circuit with pull-up resistor, that is the typical picture of an unplugged connector, a broken wire or a short to a supply voltage, and it reads as a converter far colder than possible. No manufacturer documents P0E5B publicly. Ford's limit for its sensor C, the boost converter inductor sensor, lies at 4.86 V; above that a fault is logged, yet Ford reports it as P0E59. Range checks of this kind are mandatory under CARB for hybrid inputs. Since a cold reading would hide real overheating, the controller treats the converter temperature as unknown and usually limits power. A connector check is the obvious first step. P0E5A is the low-signal counterpart.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or sensor wire broken
Signal shorted to a supply voltage
Thermistor open internally

symptoms: Hybrid system warning
Power limited as a precaution

P0E5C.title: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E5C.description: P0E5C flags a sensor C signal that changes faster than the part it watches could heat or cool. A converter inductor or heat sink has thermal mass, so a jump of many degrees within a few milliseconds points to a contact problem in the circuit, not to the converter itself. No manufacturer documents P0E5C publicly. The sensor is known from Ford, where sensor C watches the boost converter inductor and is checked only through P0E59 with fixed voltage and temperature limits; an erratic check is not described there. CARB requires hybrid input components to be monitored for circuit faults. Typical causes are a loose terminal, vibration damage or moisture at the converter connector. The fault may come and go between drives, so a wiggle test with live data helps more than a static measurement.

causes.label: Loose or widened terminal at the sensor or converter connector
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Chafed wire with intermittent contact

symptoms: Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Short episodes of reduced electric power

P0E5D.title: DC/DC Converter Enable Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E5D.description: P0E5D adds the intermittent case to the DC/DC converter enable codes P0A11 (open), P0A12 (low) and P0A13 (high). Through the enable line a hybrid or body controller switches the converter on and off; if that line flickers, the converter keeps stopping and restarting. Converter data sheets show how simple the input often is: on Poclain's 48 V unit the converter runs while the enable pin is tied to input positive or left floating and shuts off when it is pulled to input negative, so a poor ground or chafed wire can cycle it. No manufacturer documents P0E5D publicly. Ford's hybrid summaries use only P0A11 and attach several internal boost converter faults to it. CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults. The driver may see the 12 V voltage dip or a battery warning that comes and goes.

causes.label: Loose or corroded terminal on the enable line
Poor ground reference between controller and converter
Chafed enable wire touching ground intermittently
Output stage in the commanding controller faulty

symptoms: 12 V battery warning that comes and goes
Fluctuating system voltage, flickering lights
Hybrid warning, possibly reduced power

P0E5E.title: Battery Charger Control Module A Processor Performance
P0E5E.description: P0E5E reports that the processor of the on-board charger's control unit fails its self-tests. Mitsubishi spells this out for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: P0E5E-00 means a ROM checksum (CRC) error or a RAM read/write error in the charger control; the code lights both the PHEV warning and the MIL. In the Volkswagen group the code is stored by the battery management module (address 8C). Bentley's information 2066497/1 for the 2021 Bentayga Hybrid lists it with charger faults when the car will not charge or stops charging, and the remedy there is a new on-board charger (AX4). Audi's on-car analysis list of June 2026 names P0E5E00 for Q5 PHEV 2024–2025 with a check engine light after charging and asks dealers to contact technical support. Non-processor faults of the module are P0D67.

causes.label: Control electronics of the on-board charger defective (unit replacement)
Corrupt or outdated charger software
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the charger during start-up

symptoms: Plug-in charging impossible or interrupted
MIL and hybrid/PHEV warning, sometimes right after charging

P0E5F.title: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature A Too High
P0E5F.description: P0E5F is not a sensor fault: the coupler temperature sensor A works, but the charging inlet really got too hot. Three makers document it. Ford links it on the 2021–2023 Mustang Mach-E (stored in the SOBDM) to a red flashing charge indicator and no charging from a 48 A level 2 station, while 32 A or less may still work; SSM 51866 calls for a new charge port. GM's PIT5904 for the 2022 Hummer EV and BrightDrop EV600 says the pin temperatures are watched all the time and that, once the code has tripped, charging resumes only after the plug is pulled and reinserted, even when the pins have cooled; worn station plugs are a suspect. Mercedes stores P0E5F97 in the AC charger of several 2024 plug-in hybrids in strong sun and calls it no fault, with power cut back until the temperature drops.

causes.label: Excessive contact resistance in the vehicle charge port (Ford replaces the port)
Worn or damaged plug of the charging cable or station
High ambient temperature or direct sun while charging (Mercedes)
Charging control software (GM update announced)

symptoms: Charging stops or runs at reduced power
Charge indicator red or flashing red, warning in app or cluster
Charging restarts only after unplugging and replugging

P0E60.title: Battery Charge Mode Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E60.description: P0E60 concerns a wired control line that tells the on-board charger which mode to run in, set by the module that coordinates charging. Range/Performance means the line shows a valid level, but its state or response disagrees with the command. No manufacturer documents P0E60 or the modes it selects publicly. The closest documented analogue is GM's charger control circuit P0E65 in the 2016 Volt and the 2019 hybrid tables, a separate command line checked by a hardware fault flag (30 failures in 40 samples, Type B), and Ford's P0E64, which flags a missing ready answer after the charge wake-up line goes high. Under CARB, a plug-in hybrid must notice charger faults that block charging or cut its rate. Expect charging to fail, run in the wrong mode or stop, depending on how the maker has defined the modes.

causes.label: High resistance or damage on the mode control line
Input stage of the on-board charger faulty
Output stage or software of the commanding module faulty

symptoms: Plug-in charging does not start or stops
Charging runs at an unexpected rate

P0E61.title: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit/Open
P0E61.description: P0E61 means the 12 V enable line that wakes or permits the on-board charger has a circuit fault, most often an open. GM documents it codegenau. In the 2016 Volt the VICM watches this charger enable circuit; in the 2019 hybrid tables the HPC2 module does so. The test reads a fault flag reported by the driver hardware and runs when system voltage is at least 10.2 V; 30 failed samples out of 40, taken every 25 ms, set the code as Type B, so the MIL lights after two trips with the fault. GM also uses P0E61 as a blocking condition: while it is active, the high-voltage battery heater test is not run. CARB's charger rule for plug-in hybrids covers exactly such failures. With no enable signal the charger stays off and plug-in charging fails.

causes.label: Enable wire open or connector at charger/module not seated
Output driver in the controlling module (VICM/HPC2) faulty
Enable input of the on-board charger defective

symptoms: Plug-in charging does not start
MIL on after two trips
Battery heating in cold weather may be unavailable

P0E62.title: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit Low
P0E62.description: P0E62 reports that the enable line of on-board charger A is held at a lower level than its commanded state allows, typically by a short to ground. If the module drives the line high to permit charging, the charger never sees the request. Should the line instead carry a low-active signal, a grounded wire could leave the charger permitted at all times, which is why manufacturers separate low from high. No manufacturer documents P0E62 publicly. GM's 2016 Volt and 2019 hybrid tables cover only the generic enable fault P0E61, using a hardware fault flag at 10.2 V or more, 30 failures in 40 samples and Type B. CARB requires plug-in hybrids to catch charger faults that prevent charging. A shorted enable wire can also overload the driver stage in the commanding module.

causes.label: Enable wire chafed and shorted to ground
Enable input of the charger shorted internally
Driver stage in the commanding module faulty

symptoms: Charging does not start when plugged in
Charging system warning

P0E63.title: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit High
P0E63.description: P0E63 is the high-level counterpart: the enable signal to charger A sits above the level its commanded state allows, for instance because it touches a 12 V feed. In practice the charger may then be woken although no charging is requested, which can drain the 12 V battery while parked, or it may ignore a switch-off command. No manufacturer documents P0E63 publicly. GM documents only the generic enable fault P0E61 for the 2016 Volt (VICM) and in the 2019 hybrid tables (HPC2), evaluated via a hardware fault flag with 30 failures in 40 samples as Type B; separate low and high codes are not listed there. CARB counts any charger fault that disturbs charging as one a plug-in hybrid must detect. A wire chafed against a powered harness or an internal short in the charger are the usual suspects.

causes.label: Enable wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Enable input of the charger faulty
Driver stage in the commanding module stuck on

symptoms: 12 V battery drained while parked
Charger active or charging not ending as expected
Charging system warning

P0E64.title: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit Range/Performance
P0E64.description: P0E64 covers an enable line that is electrically intact while the charger still does not respond as it should. Ford documents it in its 2019 hybrid OBD summary, there titled Battery Charger Enable Circuit Range/Performance: the check runs once the charger is in its ready state and the charge wake-up signal Chrg_Wkup has gone high, and it fails when the battery energy control module still reports not ready after 30 seconds. The same monitor group checks the charger's output power against the expected value under P0D20. A BECM that does not wake, a slow start-up of either module or software disagreement between charger and BECM can therefore set P0E64 without any wiring fault. For plug-in hybrids, CARB demands detection of such charging failures. Open, low and high circuit faults are P0E61 to P0E63.

causes.label: Charger and BECM do not complete start-up within 30 s (software or wake-up timing)
Battery energy control module not waking or not reporting ready
High resistance on the wake-up line producing a marginal level

symptoms: Charging does not start although the cable is connected
Charging system warning or charge port light shows a fault

P0E65.title: Battery Charger Control Circuit/Open
P0E65.description: P0E65 flags a fault on the wired command line through which the hybrid control unit operates the on-board charger, most often an interrupted line. GM uses it codegenau: in the 2016 Volt the VICM runs the test, in the 2019 hybrid tables (19OBDG01) the HPC2 module. The check relies on a fault flag raised by the output driver hardware itself and only runs while system voltage is 10.2 V or higher and the charger enable mask is active. Samples are taken every 25 ms; 30 bad ones among 40 store the code. GM classes it Type B, so the MIL comes on once the fault returns on a second trip. Low, high and plausibility faults on the same line have their own codes, P0E66 to P0E68. Plug-in charging is usually refused until the line is repaired.

causes.label: Broken or disconnected charger control wire
Corroded or pushed-out terminal at charger or control unit
Defective output driver in the commanding control unit

symptoms: Vehicle does not charge when plugged in
MIL after the second trip with the fault (GM)
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster

P0E66.title: Battery Charger Control Circuit Low
P0E66.description: With P0E66 the controller finds the charger command line pulled lower than the state it is driving, which typically means the wire touches ground somewhere between the control unit and the on-board charger. If the command is active-high, the charger simply never receives it; a grounded line can also overload the output stage that drives it. No manufacturer documents P0E66 publicly. GM's Volt and 2019 hybrid tables check this line only through the general code P0E65, based on a hardware fault flag sampled every 25 ms at 10.2 V or more. California's OBD rule requires plug-in hybrids to recognise charger faults that stop or limit charging. P0E67 is the opposite case, a line stuck high; P0E68 covers a line that is electrically sound but answers wrongly.

causes.label: Control wire chafed through to body ground
Moisture in a connector bridging the signal to ground
Internal short in the charger's command input

symptoms: Charging does not start after plugging in
Charge indicator shows a fault or goes out

P0E67.title: Battery Charger Control Circuit High
P0E67.description: P0E67 is set when the charger command line reads higher than commanded, for instance close to battery voltage while the control unit is holding it off. A short to a live wire is the classic cause; with some driver designs an open line also floats high and lands here. The risk is the reverse of P0E66: depending on how the signal is defined, the charger may see a permanent request and try to start, or the module may stop charging as a precaution. No manufacturer documents P0E67 publicly. GM covers the line in the 2016 Volt (VICM) only with the general code P0E65, Type B, 30 of 40 samples at 25 ms. CARB expects a plug-in hybrid to detect charger malfunctions that disable or restrict charging, which applies here as well.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to a battery feed or other supply
Open line read as high by the driver circuit
Output stage of the control unit stuck switched on

symptoms: Charging aborted or not offered at all
Charger wakes up or runs without a charging request

P0E68.title: Battery Charger Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E68.description: P0E68 is the plausibility code of the charger command line: no short or open is present, yet the charger does not react to the command in the expected way or in the expected time. Typical triggers are a charger that wakes too slowly, a voltage drop on the line that leaves the level ambiguous, or software in the two modules that disagrees. No manufacturer documents P0E68 publicly. A close analogue is Ford's P0E64 on its 2019 hybrids: once the charge wake-up line is high, the battery energy control module must report ready within 30 seconds. GM's general circuit code for the same line is P0E65. CARB requires detection of charger faults that block charging or reduce its rate. Pure wiring faults are P0E65 to P0E67; a software update is often the first step.

causes.label: Charger and control unit software not matching
Charger responding late or not at all to the command
Excess resistance in the line distorting the signal level

symptoms: Charging starts late, stops or fails intermittently
Charge timer or scheduled charging not working

P0E69.title: Control Pilot Indicator Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E69.description: P0E69 belongs to the output that drives the small lamp or LED showing the state of the pilot connection to the charging station. Range/Performance means the driver circuit reports a state that does not fit what the module commanded, without a clear short or open. No manufacturer documents P0E69 publicly. GM's Volt tables for 2011 and 2012 show how such a driver is watched, under the older code P0D2B: one sample every 100 ms, a ground short counted while the LED is commanded on with the cord plugged in (12 of 15 samples), a short to battery or an open while it is off and unplugged (40 of 50), Type B. Today the hard faults are split into P0D2B, P0E3D and P0E3E. The pilot signal itself is not affected; charging usually works, only the indication is wrong.

causes.label: Indicator LED aged or partially failed, drawing the wrong current
Loose contact at the charge port lamp connector
Faulty feedback of the LED driver in the control unit

symptoms: Charge port indicator flickers, stays dark or shows the wrong state
Charging itself usually unaffected

P0E6A.title: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Circuit
P0E6A.description: P0E6A is the general code for the precharge contactor of the battery charging system. Before the main charging contactors close, this small contactor feeds the charger side through a resistor so the voltage can rise gently towards pack voltage; without it the main contacts would arc. The code collects faults of this branch that fit none of the more specific siblings. No manufacturer documents P0E6A publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables watch the same function under their own codes: the charger bus must reach 95 to 105 percent of pack voltage within 0.7 seconds (P0D26), and battery current above 3 A for about 87 ms during precharge sets P3061, both Type A. CARB requires charger malfunctions that block charging to be detected. Stuck faults are P0E6B and P0E6C, coil circuit faults P0E6D to P0E70.

causes.label: Precharge resistor burnt open or overheated
Worn or sluggish precharge contactor in the charging path
Charger-side voltage measurement reading wrongly

symptoms: Charging session aborts right at the start
Charging not possible, driving usually still possible

P0E6B.title: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed
P0E6B.description: P0E6B means the precharge contactor of the charging system appears to stay closed although it has been told to open, usually because its contacts have welded. The battery management notices this when the charger side carries voltage before any precharge was requested, or when it does not drop after switch-off. That is a safety matter: the charging path may remain live. No manufacturer documents P0E6B publicly. Mitsubishi's i-MiEV manual, published as a 2019 bulletin, handles the comparable weld of its charging contactor under P0AE2 and checks it as the high-voltage system is activated; besides wiring and the contactor itself it lists the combined charger and DC-DC unit and other high-voltage loads as possible causes. CARB requires faults that disable charging to be detected. The opposite fault is P0E6C.

causes.label: Precharge contactor contacts welded together
Coil kept energised by a control line fault
Residual voltage from another high-voltage unit misread as a closed contactor

symptoms: Charging blocked and high-voltage warning displayed
Vehicle may refuse to switch to ready mode

P0E6C.title: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
P0E6C.description: P0E6C reports that the precharge contactor of the charging system does not close, or that no current flows through the precharge branch, even though the command was given. The charger side then cannot be brought up to pack voltage, the main charging contactors stay open and the session ends before any energy flows. No manufacturer documents P0E6C publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables show the measurable symptom under other codes: if the charger bus is still outside 95 to 105 percent of pack voltage after 0.7 seconds, P0D26 is set, and if charger voltage stays under 10 V once a precharge attempt has failed, GM blames the positive charging contactor with P0D09, both Type A. CARB counts such charging failures among the faults a plug-in hybrid must detect. A welded contactor is P0E6B instead.

causes.label: Open precharge resistor interrupting the branch
Burnt or contaminated contactor contacts not conducting
Contactor coil not pulling in due to low supply

symptoms: Charging stops a few seconds after plugging in
Repeated clicking from the battery area at charge start

P0E6D.title: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit/Open
P0E6D.description: P0E6D concerns the low-voltage side of the charging precharge contactor: the coil circuit through which the control unit switches it, typically interrupted. Unlike P0E6C, which judges what happens on the high-voltage side, this code comes from the driver output itself. No manufacturer documents P0E6D publicly. GM uses the same method on the positive charging contactor of its 2019 hybrids (P0D0A): an open is recognised when the switched-off output still shows more than 4 V, or when less than 194 mA flows with the output on; 40 failed samples out of 50 at 12.5 ms set a Type B code. Mitsubishi's i-MiEV compares a coil monitor with the command and stores P0AE6 for the charging contactor. Range, low and high faults of the coil circuit are P0E6E to P0E70.

causes.label: Broken coil control wire or unplugged connector
Open winding in the contactor coil
Failed driver stage in the battery management unit

symptoms: Charging cannot be started
High-voltage system fault message

P0E6E.title: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E6E.description: P0E6E is stored when the coil circuit of the charging precharge contactor neither shows a clean short nor an open, but its electrical behaviour does not match the command: coil current outside the expected window, a slow pull-in, or feedback that lags behind the switching command. Rising contact resistance in the connector, a coil with changed resistance or a weak supply to the driver are typical. No manufacturer documents P0E6E publicly. Related GM monitoring in the 2019 hybrid tables shows the measured quantity, a current sense feedback of the contactor driver with a 194 mA minimum while on, used there for the positive charging contactor (P0D0A). CARB requires output components to be checked for proper function, not only for circuit faults. Hard faults on the same circuit are P0E6D, P0E6F and P0E70.

causes.label: Increased contact resistance in the coil connector
Contactor coil resistance out of specification
Low supply voltage at the contactor driver

symptoms: Charging starts only on some attempts
Fault appears mostly in cold weather or with a weak 12 V battery

P0E6F.title: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit Low
P0E6F.description: P0E6F points to the coil control line of the charging precharge contactor sitting too low, most likely shorted to ground. With a high-side driver the coil then cannot be energised, so precharge never starts; the driver itself may shut down to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P0E6F publicly. GM notes for the comparable high-side monitor of its positive charging contactor (P0D0A, 2019 hybrid tables) that it cannot detect a short to ground at all, which is why a separate low code makes sense. Mitsubishi's i-MiEV stores P0AE6 when the coil feedback of its charging contactor stays off while the module commands it on; it names wiring, the contactor and the EV-ECU as causes. P0E70 is the high counterpart, P0E6D an open coil circuit.

causes.label: Coil control wire shorted to ground inside or near the battery
Shorted turns in the contactor coil
Driver stage switched off by its overcurrent protection

symptoms: Charging does not start, contactor click missing
High-voltage fault message when plugging in

P0E70.title: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit High
P0E70.description: P0E70 is the high-side counterpart of P0E6F: the coil line of the charging precharge contactor carries voltage although the driver is off. A short to a 12 V feed can energise the coil without a command, which would let the precharge branch conduct unasked; the battery management therefore usually locks out charging. No manufacturer documents P0E70 publicly. For its positive charging contactor GM tests exactly this case in the 2019 hybrid tables (P0D0A): with the driver off, an output voltage above the 12 V battery voltage minus 0.4 V counts as a short to power, confirmed by 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B. Mitsubishi's i-MiEV sets P0AE7 when the coil monitor stays on after an off command. An open coil circuit is P0E6D.

causes.label: Coil control wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Driver stage in the battery management unit stuck on
Open ground return of the coil leaving the line at supply level

symptoms: Charging locked out with a high-voltage fault message
Contactor clicks without a charging request

P0E71.title: Generator Torque Delivered Performance
P0E71.description: P0E71 compares the torque that the hybrid generator or motor-generator actually provides with the value requested by the hybrid control. If the two drift apart beyond a calibrated margin, the code is set. Ford uses it codegenau in its 2024 to 2025 gasoline OBD summary: in the three-byte format P0E71-48 replaces the older P061B for a motor torque plausibility error on vehicles with the modular hybrid transmission (MHT), rated MIL plus wrench lamp. The monitor runs continuously and needs less than one second to register a fault. Under CARB, powertrain components whose failure can raise emissions fall under the comprehensive component checks. Causes range from inverter faults and position sensor errors to winding damage. Expect reduced power, limited hybrid operation or a disabled hybrid system.

causes.label: Fault in the inverter stage feeding the generator
Rotor position sensor (resolver) delivering a wrong angle
Control software needing an update
Damaged generator winding or internal contamination

symptoms: MIL and service wrench lamp on (Ford)
Reduced power or emergency running mode
Engine runs more often, hybrid assistance missing

P0E72.title: Control Pilot Signal Low Frequency
P0E72.description: P0E72 refers to the pulse train that an AC charging station places onto the pilot wire. Under SAE J1772, matched by IEC 61851-1, this is a rectangular ±12 V signal at 1 kHz, and its duty cycle tells the car how much current it may draw. The vehicle measures the period of this signal; if it is clearly slower than 1 kHz, the reading is distrusted and P0E72 is stored, because a wrong frequency also makes the current limit unreliable. No manufacturer documents P0E72 publicly. A US Department of Energy test report on pilot-line communication (PNNL) treats the 1000 Hz frequency and pulse width as values that added equipment must not disturb. Causes are a faulty station or adapter, interference on the line, or the car's measuring circuit. P0E73 is the high case; voltage faults are P0CF4 to P0CF6.

causes.label: Charging station or portable charger generating an off-spec pilot
Faulty charging adapter or extension in the cable path
Pilot measuring circuit in the vehicle charger misreading

symptoms: AC charging does not start or stops at one station
Charging works normally at other stations

P0E73.title: Control Pilot Signal High Frequency
P0E73.description: P0E73 is set when the control pilot pulses from the charging station arrive faster than the nominal 1 kHz. Above the permitted band the vehicle can no longer be sure that it decodes the duty cycle, and with it the allowed charging current, correctly; in practice it refuses or ends the session. Short spikes or ringing on the pilot line can mimic extra edges and be counted as a higher frequency, so cable condition and nearby interference matter as much as the station itself. No manufacturer documents P0E73 publicly. Simulation notes from Typhoon HIL describe the station side of this interface, a PWM signal of ±12 V at 1 kHz evaluated by a resistor network in the car. If the fault follows the vehicle across several stations, check the charge port and the charger's input. P0E72 is the low case.

causes.label: Electrical interference or ringing on the pilot line
Charging station with a faulty pilot oscillator
Damaged charging cable or corroded charge port pin
Faulty pilot input in the on-board charger

symptoms: AC charging refused or stopped shortly after start
Fault tied to a specific station or cable

P0E74.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Internal Isolation Fault
P0E74.description: P0E74 reports that the insulation between the cells or internal high-voltage parts of the traction battery and its housing has become too weak, as measured inside the pack. P0AA6, by contrast, covers isolation of the whole high-voltage system. Audi uses P0E74 codegenau: a 2018 bulletin for the A3 e-tron (model years 2017 and 2018) names it together with P0AA6 in the battery regulation control module J840, with the battery warning lamp on; workshops were asked to quarantine the car and contact technical support before replacing parts. As a reference for typical limits, GM's 2019 hybrid tables flag P0AA6 below 325,000 ohm. CARB treats high-voltage isolation detection as a safety-only system. Coolant or water inside the pack, damaged cell wiring and a faulty isolation monitor are typical.

causes.label: Coolant leak or water ingress inside the battery pack
Chafed or damaged insulation of internal high-voltage wiring
Faulty isolation measurement in the battery management

symptoms: Battery or high-voltage warning lamp on
Vehicle may not enter ready mode or blocks charging
Electric driving disabled

P0E75.title: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P0E75.description: P0E75 is the basic electrical code for coolant bypass valve A: the control unit finds that the output switching the valve, or the wire leading to it, does not form a closed circuit, in most cases because of an open. Valves of this kind usually divert coolant between loops, for example between the engine and a heater loop that keeps the cabin warm while a hybrid drives electrically. No manufacturer documents P0E75 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid and plug-in summary watches a comparable valve under the older codes P2682 and P2683 and relies on the fault status of its smart driver, which must persist beyond 5 s. CARB counts such actuators among the comprehensive components that need circuit checks. Low, high and plausibility faults of this circuit are P0E76 to P0E78; drivers mostly notice weaker heating.

causes.label: Broken wire or loose connector on the valve A control circuit
Burnt or internally open coil/motor in valve A
Coolant or water ingress corroding the valve connector pins
Faulty output driver in the engine or hybrid control module

symptoms: Check engine light
Little or no cabin heat, especially in electric mode
Engine warms up more slowly or runs more often than usual

P0E76.title: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Low
P0E76.description: With P0E76 the voltage on the control line of coolant bypass valve A stays lower than the driver expects for its current state, which points to a short to ground somewhere in the harness or inside the actuator. What happens next depends on the driver layout: a low-side output may leave the valve energised all the time, a high-side output can no longer move it at all, and the driver may switch off to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P0E76 publicly. In Ford's 2019 hybrid summary the matching job falls to P2682, flagged once the driver has signalled a fault continuously for over 5 s; only after that does Ford run its stuck-valve check P26AB. CARB requires circuit monitoring of output devices like this one. P0E77 is the high case, P0E75 an open; P0E79 and P0E7A cover a valve that is mechanically stuck.

causes.label: Chafed control wire touching body or engine ground
Internal short in the valve A actuator
Moisture bridging pins in the valve connector

symptoms: Check engine light
Valve stays in one position, heating behaves oddly
Possible blown fuse if the short is hard

P0E77.title: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit High
P0E77.description: P0E77 is logged when valve A's drive line carries more voltage than the driver should allow, typically because the wire has rubbed through against a 12 V feed. A low-side driver then sees battery voltage while it is trying to pull the line down and usually reports overcurrent; with some designs an open line can float high and end up here too. In either case the valve no longer follows commands reliably. No manufacturer documents P0E77 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary handles the same situation on its bypass valve as P2683, again set after more than 5 seconds of driver fault status. CARB expects such outputs to be checked for circuit faults. A grounded line is P0E76 and an interrupted one P0E75; replacing the valve without checking the harness first rarely helps.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Open circuit that the driver interprets as high
Faulty valve A actuator electronics

symptoms: Check engine light
Cabin heat unstable or missing

P0E78.title: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E78.description: P0E78 is the plausibility code for the actuator circuit of bypass valve A. Neither an open nor a short is present, yet current, feedback or response time of the actuator do not fit what the module has commanded: a coil whose resistance has drifted, a motor that labours against a sticky shaft, or a supply that sags under load. For motor-driven valves with position feedback the module may also see the valve arrive late or stop short. No manufacturer documents P0E78 publicly. Ford's hybrid summary for 2019 shows the general idea of checking the actual valve position once an electrical problem is known, under P26AB. CARB asks for functional checks of output components in addition to circuit tests. Hard electrical faults are P0E75 to P0E77; a valve that stays put is P0E79 or P0E7A.

causes.label: Deposits or wear making the valve A mechanism sluggish
High resistance at connector or ground of the valve circuit
Low supply voltage to the actuator under load

symptoms: Check engine light
Heating output varies from trip to trip

P0E79.title: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Stuck/Open
P0E79.description: P0E79 reports that bypass valve A apparently remains open although the module has asked it to close. The control unit cannot see the valve directly; it infers the position from temperatures, typically by comparing two coolant sensors that should drift apart when the loops are separated. No manufacturer documents P0E79 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary describes exactly this logic for its older code P26AB, a valve stuck in the combined loop: if the heater-loop sensor reads more than 5 °F above the engine sensor within 60 seconds after a circuit fault, the valve is taken as stuck. An open valve lets heat escape into the larger loop, so cabin heat in electric mode suffers and the engine may warm up differently. CARB requires functional monitoring of such outputs. The opposite case is P0E7A.

causes.label: Valve A jammed open by debris or a broken internal part
Actuator no longer moves the valve
Hoses swapped at the valve after a repair
Skewed coolant temperature sensor misleading the check

symptoms: Weak cabin heat in electric mode
Engine starts more often to supply heat
Check engine light

P0E7A.title: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Stuck Closed
P0E7A.description: P0E7A is the reverse of P0E79: valve A should open and let coolant pass, but the temperature picture says it has stayed shut. Depending on what the valve connects, the result is a loop that gets no flow from the engine side, so heater output or heat transfer drops, or a branch that heats up because it is cut off from circulation. No manufacturer documents P0E7A publicly. The closest published case is the sibling on valve B: Stellantis sets P0E80 once the engine coolant reading and the electric heater inlet are over 40 °F apart, and blames misrouted hoses or a clogged three-way valve on Wrangler and Pacifica plug-in hybrids. Under CARB, actuators of this kind need a functional check as well. Electrical faults on valve A are P0E75 to P0E78.

causes.label: Debris or deposits blocking valve A
Actuator or gear stuck in the closed position
Air pocket after a coolant service blocking flow

symptoms: Little or no cabin heat
Rising coolant temperature in the affected loop
Check engine light

P0E7B.title: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P0E7B.description: P0E7B covers an interrupted control circuit of the second coolant bypass valve, B. The module sees no proper load on its output, so the valve cannot be positioned and stays wherever it last was or springs back to its rest position. Stellantis does use the valve B family: its 2025 and 2026 bulletins for the RAM 1500 and the Wagoneer with the 3.0 litre Hurricane engine list P0E7C to P0E7F together with U063C, a lost link to the valve B actuator, and its plug-in hybrids use P0E7F and P0E80. P0E7B itself appears in none of these published documents. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary shows the usual circuit test on a comparable valve, a driver fault lasting over 5 seconds. CARB requires circuit checks on such outputs. Short and plausibility faults are P0E7C to P0E7E.

causes.label: Broken wire or unplugged connector at valve B
Internal open in the valve B actuator
Missing supply or ground at a networked valve actuator

symptoms: Check engine light
Heating or engine warm-up behaves differently

P0E7C.title: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Low
P0E7C.description: P0E7C says that the wiring which operates bypass valve B reads too low, typically because a wire or the actuator itself has a ground fault. Stellantis documents the code: bulletin 18-071-26 (revisions A and B, October 2026) for 2025 RAM 1500 pickups fitted with the Hurricane straight-six, SO or HO twin-turbo and bulletin 18-082-26 for the 2025 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer name it among the faults cured by new engine control software, with the check engine light on. That points to calibration as a frequent trigger on these engines, besides real wiring damage. A low reading on the line keeps the valve from being driven as intended, so the coolant split between loops is no longer under control. CARB lists such outputs among the components that need circuit monitoring. High and open faults are P0E7D and P0E7B.

causes.label: Engine control software needing the update from the manufacturer bulletin (Stellantis 3.0 Hurricane)
Valve B control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve B actuator

symptoms: Check engine light
Often no noticeable driving symptom

P0E7D.title: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit High
P0E7D.description: P0E7D is stored when the line driving valve B sits above its expected level, for instance with the wire chafed against a powered line or a driver that cannot pull the circuit down. Stellantis names this code in the same software bulletins as its low sibling: 18-071-26 for the 2025 RAM pickup with Hurricane power, plus 18-082-26 (SO engine) and 18-083-26 (HO engine) for the 2025 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer. All of them require a lit check engine light, and the fix is a reflash of the engine control module, sometimes alongside oxygen sensor and airflow codes. Before replacing hardware it is therefore worth checking for such an update. CARB expects outputs like this to be checked for circuit faults. The low case is P0E7C, an open circuit P0E7B, a networked actuator that stops talking U063C.

causes.label: Outdated engine control software (Stellantis bulletins 18-071-26, 18-082-26, 18-083-26)
Valve B control wire shorted to a voltage source
Open circuit pulled high by the module input

symptoms: Check engine light
Other stored codes after the same software issue

P0E7E.title: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E7E.description: P0E7E marks a control circuit of coolant bypass valve B that is electrically intact but does not respond as calibrated: actuator current, feedback or timing lie outside the window the software expects. Stellantis lists P0E7E most often of the valve B codes. Bulletin 18-106-25 from December 2025 covers model year 2026 RAM 1500 trucks with the high-output Hurricane built up to 7 October 2025 and calls for an engine control module update; the 2026 bulletins 18-071-26 and 18-082-26 repeat the code for the 2025 RAM and Wagoneer. Since a software fix is the documented remedy, a sluggish but working valve often turns out not to be the culprit. CARB requires functional monitoring of outputs, not only circuit checks. The pure wiring faults are P0E7B to P0E7D, mechanical sticking P0E7F and P0E80.

causes.label: Engine control calibration fixed by bulletin 18-106-25 or 18-071-26 (Stellantis)
Valve B actuator moving slowly or not reaching its target
Corroded connector raising circuit resistance

symptoms: Check engine light
Usually no change in driving behaviour

P0E7F.title: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Stuck/Open
P0E7F.description: P0E7F means coolant bypass valve B is judged to stay open while the module wants it closed. Stellantis documents it on the Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrid with the 3.6 litre engine: bulletin 07-008-23 (June 2023) covers cars built from 3 November 2022 to 10 February 2023, where machining debris from the cylinder head water jackets can collect inside the three-way valve. The MIL comes on and electric driving may be locked out while the petrol engine still works. To reproduce it, the bulletin has the car idle 10 minutes in engine mode, then run 5 minutes on battery with heat on and the blower below half; if P0E7F or P0E80 appears, the valve is replaced. The Hurricane software bulletins also list the code. P0E80 is the stuck closed case; P0E79 is the same fault on valve A.

causes.label: Machining debris lodged in the three-way coolant valve (Pacifica Hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23)
Worn or broken internals in valve B
Calibration issue addressed by an engine control update (3.0 Hurricane)

symptoms: MIL on
Electric drive mode unavailable, engine runs instead
Reduced or unstable cabin heat

P0E80.title: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Stuck Closed
P0E80.description: P0E80 reports that bypass valve B has stayed shut although flow through it is requested. Stellantis gives the criterion for the Jeep Wrangler plug-in hybrid (2021 to 2023): the code sets once engine coolant and the inlet of the electric coolant heater differ by more than 40 °F, about 22 K. Its service case S2208000205 and bulletin 07-006-23 (cars built on 4 June 2022) trace this to hoses on the three-way valve that were fitted one port off; drivers notice a lit check engine light and at times no heat, and the fix is rerouting the hoses using the marks on the valve. On the 2022 to 2023 Pacifica plug-in hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23 blames a valve clogged by machining debris and replaces it. CARB covers such outputs under functional monitoring. P0E7F is the open counterpart.

causes.label: Hoses at the three-way valve shifted by one port (Wrangler 4xe, bulletin 07-006-23)
Valve blocked by machining debris (Pacifica Hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23)
Valve B actuator seized in the closed position

symptoms: Check engine light
Intermittent loss of cabin heat
Electric mode may be disabled

P0E81.title: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0E81.description: P0E81 is the general circuit code for temperature sensor A in an auxiliary cooling loop, a coolant circuit separate from the main engine loop, such as a heater loop of a plug-in hybrid or a loop that cools electric drive parts. The module sees a signal it cannot use at all, without classing it as too low, too high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0E81 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary describes a comparable sensor, ECT2, placed between the electric PTC heater and the heater matrix, and checks its circuit through the analog input under P2184 and P2185. Volvo uses the term auxiliary cooling system for its T8 hybrids under P0EA7. CARB requires temperature sensors of this kind to be checked for circuit continuity. The more specific siblings are P0E82 to P0E84.

causes.label: Loose, corroded or unplugged sensor connector
Failed temperature sensor A
Damaged signal or reference wire

symptoms: Check engine light
Heater or auxiliary pump runs on default values

P0E82.title: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0E82.description: P0E82 is set when temperature sensor A of the auxiliary cooling loop delivers a clean electrical signal whose value does not make sense against other temperatures. No manufacturer documents P0E82 publicly, but Ford's 2019 hybrid summary spells out such a plausibility test for its heater-loop sensor ECT2 under P2183. After at least 360 minutes of soak both coolant sensors must agree within 30 °F; with the loops joined and the electric pump above 2,500 rpm for 90 seconds, ECT2 plus a 7 °F hose loss must stay within 30 °F of the engine sensor; and the reading must stay between −30 and 275 °F. CARB includes hybrid component temperature sensors in its rationality requirements. A sensor that drifts, or a stuck bypass valve that keeps the loops apart, can trip it. Pure circuit faults are P0E81, P0E83 and P0E84.

causes.label: Sensor A reading drifted out of tolerance
Stuck bypass valve keeping the loops from mixing
Low coolant or air around the sensor tip
Corroded terminals shifting the signal

symptoms: Check engine light
Cabin heat regulation off target

P0E83.title: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0E83.description: P0E83 means the signal voltage of temperature sensor A in the auxiliary cooling loop has fallen below its valid floor. Coolant sensors are normally NTC thermistors whose resistance drops as they warm, so a low voltage reads as extremely hot coolant. When the value is beyond anything physically possible, the cause is usually a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor rather than real overheating. No manufacturer documents P0E83 publicly. On Ford's 2019 hybrids the equivalent fault of the heater-loop sensor ECT2 is P2184, recorded after 5 seconds of driver fault status. CARB requires out-of-range detection for such temperature inputs. The module may then run pumps or fans on safe defaults. P0E84 is the opposite, a reading stuck cold; P0E82 covers values inside the range that are implausible.

causes.label: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Internally shorted sensor A
Genuinely very hot coolant in the auxiliary loop

symptoms: Check engine light
Coolant pump or fan running continuously
Implausibly high temperature shown on a scan tool

P0E84.title: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0E84.description: P0E84 is the high-voltage case for sensor A of the auxiliary loop: the signal sits near the reference voltage, which an NTC thermistor would only produce at extreme cold. Far more often the circuit is open, from an unplugged connector, a broken wire or a sensor with an internal break, or the signal line is shorted to a voltage source. The module then cannot judge the temperature of that loop and falls back to substitute values, which can make heater or pump control less precise. No manufacturer documents P0E84 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary uses P2185 for the equivalent fault of its heater-loop sensor ECT2, set after the driver signals a fault for 5 seconds. CARB wants temperature inputs tested for readings beyond their valid span. P0E83 is the low counterpart.

causes.label: Unplugged connector or broken sensor wire
Sensor A open internally
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

symptoms: Check engine light
Scan tool shows the loop at minimum temperature
Less precise cabin heating

P0E85.title: Battery Charger B Temperature Too High
P0E85.description: P0E85 reports that the second charger stage or second on-board charger, labelled B, has become hotter than its own protection limit allows. Like the A counterpart P0D24, it is a heat verdict, not a sensor fault: the charger trusts its reading and cuts back power or stops to save its semiconductors. No manufacturer documents P0E85 with set conditions in public sources. Toyota shows that the letter B is real hardware: the 6.6 kW charger of the RAV4 Prime logs its input current fault as charger B (P0E89). CARB asks plug-in hybrids to flag charger failures that stop charging or reduce its rate. Typical triggers are poor coolant flow or air flow, a clogged heat exchanger or an internal defect. Expect slow or aborted AC charging, not loss of drive.

causes.label: Too little coolant or air flow through charger B (low coolant, pump, blocked fins)
Internal defect in the power stage of charger B
Long full-power charging in very hot surroundings

symptoms: AC charging slows down noticeably or stops before the battery is full
Charging fault message or flashing charge-port indicator

P0E86.title: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Too Low
P0E86.description: P0E86 means charger B sees less voltage at its input than it needs to work, although charging has been requested. It mirrors P0D27, which carries no letter and is used for the first charger. No manufacturer documents P0E86 publicly. Ford's plug-in hybrid summary (OBDSM1901) does list the opposite case on the same input, P0E87, which shows that the B input codes are in real use. A low input voltage is often caused outside the car: a weak or long house circuit, a faulty extension or charging cable, or a charging station that sags under load. Inside the car, worn inlet contacts or a bad high-voltage connection to the charger can do the same. CARB does not require faults originating in the supply to be detected, so an unconfirmed code may just reflect a poor socket.

causes.label: Weak supply at the socket or charging station, long or undersized house wiring
Faulty charging cable, adapter or extension lead
Worn or burnt contacts in the charge inlet or its wiring to the charger
Voltage measurement inside charger B reads too low

symptoms: AC charging does not start or stops shortly after starting
Charging works at another socket or station

P0E87.title: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Too High
P0E87.description: P0E87 flags an input voltage for charger B above what the charger accepts. Ford uses the code in its plug-in hybrid OBD summary (OBDSM1901) in an unusual way: it is part of a plausibility test run on the battery controller (BECM) and judges the charging voltage request that reaches the charger. Once the charger is in its ready state, a requested value above 450 V counts as a fault, and the check needs less than one second. In that reading the code points to a wrong command over the network rather than to the grid, so module software and data on the bus deserve attention first. On other designs a measured overvoltage at the input would set it. Ford lets charger faults request the amber wrench lamp instead of a specific charging message. The low case is P0E86.

causes.label: Implausible charging voltage request from the battery control module (Ford logic)
Software fault in the charger or battery control module
Real overvoltage from the supply or charging station

symptoms: Charging is refused or ends early
Amber wrench lamp in the instrument cluster (Ford)

P0E88.title: Battery Charger B Input Current Too Low
P0E88.description: P0E88 is set when charger B takes in less current than it should for the charging power it is asked to deliver, with voltage present. Its counterpart without a letter is P0D29. No manufacturer documents P0E88 in public sources. The neighbour P0E89 for too much current is documented by Ford, Toyota, Isuzu and Mercedes, so the input current of a B charger is clearly monitored. A low value with normal voltage suggests that the charger does not ramp up, that a resistive inlet or cable limits the flow, or that the charging station offers less current than expected. A measurement error is possible too, but those have their own sensor codes (P0E8A). CARB requires charger faults that limit the charging rate to be detected. Usually charging is just slow; driving is not affected.

causes.label: Charger B power stage does not reach the requested power
High resistance at inlet contacts or in the charging cable
Charging station or cable signals a lower current limit than expected

symptoms: AC charging takes much longer than usual
Charging stops or a charging fault is shown

P0E89.title: Battery Charger B Input Current Too High
P0E89.description: P0E89 reports more input current into charger B than permitted, and it is the best documented code of this series. Toyota lists P0E8919 on 2021 to 2023 RAV4 Prime XSE models with the 6.6 kW charger, together with P0D2A19 and PFC boost faults; the MIL is on, plug-in charging fails and the charger assembly is replaced (T-SB-0067-22). Ford's plug-in summary sets it when the charger, in ready state, receives a charging current request above 100 A. Isuzu logs it as excessive on-board charger input current in the VCU of the 2025-2026 NRR-EV with an amber EV warning and cures it with a VCU recalibration. Mercedes uses P0E8929 in the DC charging unit of several plug-in hybrids and the eSprinter, where the vehicle may refuse to start once a DC fast charge has ended. Too little current is P0E88.

causes.label: Defective power factor correction or power stage in the charger (Toyota RAV4 Prime)
Calibration or software of the vehicle or charging control unit (Isuzu VCU, Mercedes DC charging unit, Ford request logic)
Current ripple or overcurrent from the charging station (Mercedes)

symptoms: MIL or EV system warning lamp on
Plug-in charging stops or does not work at all
Vehicle does not start after DC fast charging (Mercedes)

P0E8A.title: Battery Charger B Input Current Sensor Circuit
P0E8A.description: P0E8A concerns the measurement, not the current itself: the sensor that tells charger B how much current enters at its input delivers no usable signal. It is the general circuit code; range, low and high faults of the same sensor sit at P2D85, P2D83 and P2D84, and the sensor of charger A uses P0D38. No manufacturer documents P0E8A publicly. That the B input current is evaluated is clear from P0E89, which Toyota sets on the RAV4 Prime as a circuit current above threshold and Ford tests against a 100 A limit. CARB requires inputs such as this to be checked for open circuits and out-of-range signals. In most chargers the sensor sits inside the unit, so a confirmed fault usually means repairing or replacing the charger. Without the reading, charging is refused or stopped.

causes.label: Current sensor or its evaluation inside charger B defective
Open or shorted sensor wiring where the sensor is external
Charger software misjudges the sensor signal

symptoms: AC charging does not start or is aborted
Charging fault indication; driving remains possible

P0E8B.title: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Sensor Circuit
P0E8B.description: P0E8B covers an electrical fault in the voltage measurement at the input of charger B: the controller gets no valid reading of the supply voltage. Range, low and high faults of this sensor have their own codes, P2E84, P2E85 and P2E86; charger A uses P0D3D for its first input voltage sensor. Some code lists call it input voltage sensor A of charger B. No manufacturer documents P0E8B publicly. Ford checks the voltage side of charger B through P0E87 with a 450 V limit, which is a judgment of the value, whereas P0E8B means the value cannot be read at all. CARB expects such inputs to be monitored for circuit continuity and range. The sensing is usually built into the charger, so after ruling out connectors the charger is the likely part. Charging is blocked until the fault clears.

causes.label: Voltage sensing circuit inside charger B defective
Loose or corroded connector, damaged sensing lead
Charger software fault

symptoms: Plug-in charging is not possible
Charging fault message or charge-port indicator signals a fault

P0E8C.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit
