P0E8C.description: The inverter of drive motor A may measure its high-voltage DC level at more than one point; sensor B is the second of those channels. P0E8C is the general circuit code for it, used when the signal is missing or electrically invalid without a clear low, high or plausibility verdict. Sensor A of the same inverter uses P0D2D, and a mismatch between both is P2E1A. No manufacturer documents P0E8C itself. Mitsubishi shows what sensor B can be: in the 2023 Outlander PHEV the power drive unit reads the boosted capacitor 2 voltage on a main channel, called V2M, and assigns its faults to P0E8D to P0E8F, while capacitor 1 belongs to sensor A. CARB requires such inputs to be checked for circuit faults. Without a trusted value the controller limits or blocks electric drive.

causes.label: Sensing circuit for voltage channel B inside the power electronics defective
Low-voltage connector or harness of the inverter loose or damaged
Software fault in the motor control unit

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning together with the MIL
Reduced electric drive power or vehicle not ready to drive

P0E8D.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0E8D.description: P0E8D says that voltage sensor B of the drive motor A inverter delivers a value that is electrically fine but disagrees with other readings of the same bus. Mitsubishi details the check for the 2023 Outlander PHEV, where sensor B is the main channel at capacitor 2 (V2M): with the boost converter switched off and the unit powered with 8 V or more for 0.5 s, a gap of at least 100 V to the rear motor unit, or of at least 50 V to capacitor 1, lasting 0.2 s sets the code, and the hint points to the power drive unit. Audi lists P0E8D00 with P0C0C00 in the electric drive of 2025-2026 Q6 and A6 e-tron models; if all entries appear together with a red high-voltage warning, the power electronics are replaced. Hard circuit faults are P0E8C, P0E8E and P0E8F.

causes.label: Fault in the power electronics or its voltage measurement (Mitsubishi, Audi)
Drift of voltage channel B so that it no longer matches the other channels
Wrong reference value from another high-voltage unit (rear motor unit, battery management)

symptoms: Red high-voltage system warning at start, stop safely (Audi)
MIL and hybrid warning, reduced or no electric drive

P0E8E.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0E8E.description: P0E8E means the output of inverter voltage sensor B for drive motor A has fallen to the bottom end of its scale. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi assigns it to the main measuring channel of capacitor 2 (V2M) in the power drive unit and sets it when that signal stays at no more than 0.45 V for 0.16 s, provided the unit has at least 8 V supply; monitoring runs continuously. Electrically this matches a short to ground, a broken signal path or a sensing circuit that has died, because the high-voltage bus itself would rarely read near zero while the system is active. The same channel reading high is P0E8F, while capacitor 1 on sensor A uses P0D2F for its low case. As the controller cannot trust the bus voltage, electric drive is limited or switched off and the MIL comes on.

causes.label: Measuring circuit for capacitor 2 inside the power drive unit failed
Signal line shorted to ground or open
No high voltage on the bus because of a blown fuse or open contactor path

symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning
Vehicle not ready to drive or only engine power available

P0E8F.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit High
P0E8F.description: P0E8F is the upper-limit fault of inverter voltage sensor B on drive motor A. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV sets it when the main channel at capacitor 2 (V2M) reports at least 4.75 V for 0.16 s, again with the unit supplied at 8 V or above, and lists it as a range check maximum. A reading pinned at the top usually comes from the signal touching the sensor supply, from a lost sensor ground or from a defect in the measuring circuit. A real overvoltage of the bus cannot be ruled out, but it has its own code, P0C79, and would normally show on several channels at once; if sensor A (P0D30) and the battery voltage are normal, the B channel itself is suspect. P0E8E is the low counterpart. The controller protects the inverter by limiting or stopping electric drive.

causes.label: Measuring circuit for capacitor 2 inside the power drive unit defective
Signal shorted to sensor supply or lost sensor ground
Actual overvoltage on the high-voltage bus

symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning
Electric drive switched off or strongly reduced

P0E90.title: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E90.description: P0E90 is meant for a voltage sensor B signal of the drive motor A inverter that flickers, jumps or drops out for moments without staying wrong long enough for the low or high code. No manufacturer documents P0E90 publicly. The documented siblings show how short the window is: Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV flags the same channel (V2M at capacitor 2) as too low or too high only after 0.16 s beyond 0.45 V or 4.75 V, and as implausible after 0.2 s of deviation, so shorter glitches need an extra stability test. CARB asks for input signals to be checked for circuit and rationality faults. In practice a loose low-voltage plug on the inverter, a chafed lead or a solder joint that opens with heat and vibration is the usual cause. Warnings may appear and vanish again.

causes.label: Loose or corroded low-voltage connector on the inverter
Chafed or partly broken signal lead
Measuring circuit in the power electronics failing intermittently with heat or vibration

symptoms: Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Short power interruptions or jerky electric drive

P0E91.title: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit
P0E91.description: P0E91 is the circuit code for the second DC voltage channel, sensor B, in the inverter of drive motor B, usually the second electric machine or the rear axle motor. It applies when this signal is absent or electrically unusable without a more precise verdict; its partner channel A is coded P0DA3, and the matching code for drive motor A is P0E8C. No manufacturer documents P0E91 or its B-sensor siblings for motor B publicly. Mitsubishi illustrates the frame with sensor A of the rear motor on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the rear motor unit reports its inverter voltage, which the front power electronics compare with their own capacitor values. CARB requires inputs of hybrid drive components to be monitored for circuit faults. Motor B is then usually switched off, and the car may drive with reduced power.

causes.label: Voltage channel B measuring circuit in the motor B inverter defective
Connector or harness of the motor B inverter loose or damaged
Software fault in the motor B control unit

symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning with MIL
Loss of the second drive motor (for example no all-wheel drive), reduced power

P0E92.title: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0E92.description: P0E92 is stored when voltage sensor B of the drive motor B inverter gives a reading inside its electrical range that does not fit the other voltage values of the high-voltage system. No manufacturer documents P0E92 publicly. The closest published test is Mitsubishi's plausibility check P0DA4, written for the first voltage channel of the rear motor in the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with the boost converter off, the rear inverter voltage is compared with capacitor 1 and both capacitor 2 channels of the front unit, and a difference of 100 V or more to each of them for 0.2 s counts; the hints name the rear motor unit, battery management and the power drive unit. For drive motor A the same fault on sensor B is P0E8D. A drifting measurement or a wrong reference elsewhere are both possible, so all channels should be compared.

causes.label: Voltage channel B of the motor B inverter drifts
Internal fault of the motor B inverter or motor unit
Wrong comparison value from battery management or the front power electronics

symptoms: MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
Second drive motor switched off, reduced acceleration

P0E93.title: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0E93.description: With P0E93 the controller sees the B voltage channel in the motor B inverter stuck near the bottom of its signal range, as happens with a short to ground, an open signal path or a failed measuring circuit. No manufacturer documents P0E93 publicly. Mitsubishi's rear motor sensor A on the 2023 Outlander PHEV gives a comparable limit: its low code P0DA5 sets once the signal sits at or below 0.55 V for 0.3 s with the rear motor unit powered at 8 V or more, and the checks start with the battery management and the high-voltage cables to the rear motor before the motor unit itself. Drive motor A has the equivalent sensor B fault as P0E8E. If several channels read low together, missing high voltage is more likely than a sensor fault. Motor B is normally disabled until the reading is valid.

causes.label: Measuring circuit for channel B in the motor B inverter failed
Signal line shorted to ground or open
High-voltage cable or connection to motor B open, no voltage at the inverter

symptoms: MIL and EV system warning
Rear or second motor without power, front-drive only

P0E94.title: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit High
P0E94.description: P0E94 records that voltage sensor B in the drive motor B inverter reports a value at the top of its signal range. A short from the signal to a supply, an interrupted sensor ground or a defective measuring stage are the usual explanations; a genuine overvoltage would normally show on the other channels too. No manufacturer documents P0E94 publicly. For sensor A of the rear motor Mitsubishi publishes the high limit on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: P0DA6 needs a signal of at least 4.76 V lasting 0.3 s, and only while the propulsion system is active, so the check is not run in standby. The low side of sensor B on motor B is P0E93, the high side of sensor B on motor A is P0E8F. CARB requires out-of-range checks for such inputs. Expect the second motor to be taken offline and a warning with MIL.

causes.label: Measuring stage for channel B in the motor B inverter defective
Signal shorted to a supply or lost sensor ground
Real overvoltage on the high-voltage bus

symptoms: MIL and EV system warning
Second drive motor deactivated, less traction and power

P0E95.title: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E95.description: P0E95 closes the sensor B series for drive motor B: the signal is unstable, with brief dropouts or spikes, rather than permanently low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0E95 publicly. Published values for the neighbouring channels show why short events slip through the other tests: Mitsubishi rates sensor A of the rear motor (2023 Outlander PHEV) as low or high only after 0.3 s outside 0.55 V to 4.76 V, and its plausibility check needs 0.2 s of large deviation. CARB expects inputs to be monitored for circuit, range and rationality faults. Because a rear motor and its wiring are exposed to road spray and suspension movement, a corroded or loose connector is the first thing to check. The warning may appear only on rough roads and clear itself later.

causes.label: Corroded or loose connector on the motor B inverter
Harness damaged where it moves with the axle or suspension
Measuring circuit in the motor B inverter failing intermittently

symptoms: EV or hybrid warning that appears and clears again
Second motor drops out briefly, uneven traction

P0E96.title: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit
P0E96.description: P0E96 opens the series for a third voltage measurement in a DC/DC converter, sensor C. It is the general circuit code, meant for a missing or electrically invalid signal; range, low, high and erratic faults of the same sensor follow from P0E97 to P0E9A. Where a converter has more than two voltage channels, for example input and output plus a redundant reading, C names the third. No manufacturer documents P0E96 or any sensor C code in public sources. For orientation, GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) cover sensors A and B of a 12 V converter that supports engine auto-starts, with valid readings between 1 V and 28 V and Type B confirmation; FCA calls the first two channels voltage sensor 1 and 2. CARB asks for circuit faults of such inputs to be detected. Converter output may be cut back.

causes.label: Measuring circuit for channel C inside the converter defective
Loose connector or damaged sensing lead
Software fault in the converter or its controller

symptoms: 12 V or converter warning, possibly with MIL
Start-stop or 12 V support restricted

P0E97.title: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0E97.description: P0E97 is the plausibility code for the third voltage channel of a DC/DC converter: sensor C delivers an electrically valid value that does not agree with what the controller expects. Two makers document it. Audi names P0E9700 for the 2020-2021 Q5 and 2021 A7 plug-in hybrids, stored now and then by the J841 electronics of the electric drive, with symptom code 45146; the revised bulletin explains that the software ignored the tolerance of two capacitors, so the ratio between capacity A and B fell outside its limit, and new software (version 0102) cures it. Mercedes-Benz lists P0E9700 for the converter of the EQB and the G-Class after a faulty wake-up of that unit. Hard faults of sensor C are P0E96, P0E98 and P0E99.

causes.label: Converter or power electronics software with too tight plausibility limits
Converter stuck in an error state after an incorrect wake-up
Drifting voltage measurement inside the converter

symptoms: MIL on, often without a noticeable driving fault
12 V battery or high-voltage warning messages in the cluster
Fault entry appears sporadically and returns after clearing

P0E98.title: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit Low
P0E98.description: P0E98 is set when the C voltage channel of a DC/DC converter is stuck at the lowest end of its range, typically because the measuring line is grounded or the sensing stage has lost its supply. No manufacturer documents P0E98 publicly. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A) show the matching test on channels A and B of the 12 V stabiliser used for auto-starts: below 1 V in 320 out of 400 readings at a 12.5 ms rate gives P0E33 or P0E38, rated Type B. A third channel would be judged the same way. CARB calls for range monitoring of inputs like this. If the converter output itself is normal on the other channels, the fault lies in the C path. The high counterpart is P0E99.

causes.label: Sensor C signal line shorted to ground
Measuring stage without supply or with an open signal path
Internal defect in the converter's measuring circuit

symptoms: MIL on, depending on the manufacturer's rating
Converter output reduced or switched to a fallback value
Start-stop or 12 V support may be disabled

P0E99.title: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit High
P0E99.description: With P0E99 the controller finds the voltage sensor C reading of a DC/DC converter pinned near its upper limit. That points to the signal touching a battery feed or reference supply, or to a broken sensor ground that lets the input float up, rather than to a real converter overvoltage. No manufacturer documents P0E99 publicly. For channels A and B GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) use more than 28 V as the limit for a 12 V converter, far beyond any genuine output, and confirm P0E34 or P0E39 after 320 of 400 failed samples as Type B. CARB demands such out-of-range checks. Comparing sensor C with the other channels and the battery voltage quickly separates a wiring fault from a converter problem; low readings are P0E98.

causes.label: Sensor C signal shorted to battery voltage or reference supply
Open sensor ground letting the signal float high
Actual overvoltage from a faulty converter regulation

symptoms: MIL and charging or 12 V warning possible
Converter limits or stops its output
Start-stop function unavailable

P0E9A.title: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E9A.description: P0E9A completes the sensor C voltage series of a DC/DC converter. It is meant for a signal that jumps, flickers or drops out for brief moments, which the low and high tests miss because they need a fault to persist. No manufacturer documents P0E9A publicly. The GM tables for channels A and B (25OBDG03A) illustrate the gap: their limit checks sample every 12.5 ms and require 320 failures in a window of 400, roughly four seconds, before a code is stored. Under CARB rules inputs need circuit and range tests and, if possible, a check for implausible values; an erratic code covers the cases in between. Corroded pins, a solder joint with a hairline crack or a wire that rubs through under engine movement are the usual causes, so the warning may come and go.

causes.label: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor C path
Harness chafing intermittently at a moving point
Cracked solder joint in the converter's measuring circuit

symptoms: Warning lamp that appears and disappears
Short interruptions of start-stop or 12 V support
Code often stored as history only

P0E9B.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit
P0E9B.description: P0E9B opens the series for the second current measurement of a DC/DC converter, sensor B. It covers a signal that is absent or unusable on the electrical level and that the controller cannot classify as low, high or implausible; those cases follow as P0E9C to P0E9F. No manufacturer documents P0E9B itself. Porsche confirms what sensor B is in practice: on the Taycan the high-voltage power electronics name the same channel current sensor 2 and store its short to ground as P0E9D00. Ford's hybrid summary shows what a current input check looks at, an offset below 15 A at power-up and a raw value kept inside 4.5-6.0 V. CARB makes circuit monitoring of such inputs mandatory. Without the reading the converter usually derates.

causes.label: Fault in the converter's internal current sensing
Connector or wiring fault on the sensor B path
Control software misjudging the signal

symptoms: High-voltage or 12 V system warning
Converter output reduced, 12 V battery charged less
Possibly reduced drive power

P0E9C.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0E9C.description: P0E9C means current sensor B of a DC/DC converter gives a value within its electrical window that does not match the operating state, for example a current that stays put while the load changes, or that differs from the figure the controller derives from voltages and switching. No manufacturer documents P0E9C publicly. Ford describes such a rationality test for the boost converter of its hybrids under P0A94: a gap above 50 A between calculated and measured inductor current, lasting over 4 s in controlled operation, flags the converter. FCA treats the equivalent sensor A code P0E52 on the Ram 1500 eTorque as a one-trip fault after a software update. Circuit faults of sensor B are P0E9B, P0E9D and P0E9E.

causes.label: Current sensor B drifting or with a shifted zero point
Fault in the converter power stage causing unexpected currents
Software with an unsuitable plausibility window

symptoms: MIL, sometimes after a single trip
Reduced converter output and weak 12 V charging
Power reduction warning possible

P0E9D.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit Low
P0E9D.description: P0E9D reports that the signal of DC/DC converter current sensor B has dropped below its valid range. Porsche documents it for the Taycan of model years 2020 to 2024 as P0E9D00, current sensor 2 of the converter with a short to ground, logged by the HV power electronics on the front axle (A49), the rear axle (A50) or both. A red warning tells the driver to stop safely because of an electrical fault, yet once the ignition has been cycled the entry is no longer active. Porsche blames a diagnostic threshold for current monitoring that was set too low and reprograms both control units, using PIWIS Tester version 43.500.000 or newer. Outside that case a real ground short or a dead sensor supply is the likely cause. The high counterpart is P0E9E.

causes.label: Current monitoring threshold set too low in the software
Sensor B signal shorted to ground
Sensor supply missing inside the power electronics

symptoms: Red warning to stop the vehicle safely
Fault no longer active after an ignition cycle
Drive power reduced or vehicle not ready to drive

P0E9E.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit High
P0E9E.description: P0E9E flags the B current channel of a DC/DC converter reading above its ceiling: the raw signal lies above anything the sensor should output. With a Hall sensor whose zero lies mid-scale, this usually means the signal line touches the supply or the reference ground has opened. No manufacturer documents P0E9E publicly. Mercedes-Benz shows the same fault type on the first channel: on the EQB and G-Class, P0E5400 denotes a short to battery plus on the converter's current sensor A and shows up with red 12 V and HV warnings after a faulty wake-up; the workshop checks it with a buck-mode test of about 30 s in XENTRY and then resets the converter. Porsche calls the B channel current sensor 2 and has its low fault as P0E9D. A real overcurrent belongs to P0D33.

causes.label: Sensor B signal shorted to supply voltage
Open reference ground of the current sensor
Converter in an error state after wake-up, cleared by reset

symptoms: Red 12 V battery or HV warning
Converter stops supplying the 12 V network
Reduced drive power possible

P0E9F.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E9F.description: P0E9F is reserved for a current sensor B signal of a DC/DC converter that is unsteady: it spikes, drops out or shows noise yet never stays out of bounds for long. Publicly, no maker describes P0E9F. The Porsche case on the same channel shows how hard such events are to pin down: the Taycan's current sensor 2 low fault P0E9D00 is no longer active after an ignition cycle, and the remedy was a revised threshold rather than a part. Ford rates a current signal as valid only inside a raw band of 4.5-6.0 V; a value that leaves and re-enters that band briefly is exactly what an erratic code is for. CARB asks for inputs to be watched for open, shorted and implausible signals. Loose terminals, vibration or a marginal solder joint are typical; steady low or high faults are P0E9D and P0E9E.

causes.label: Loose terminal or connector on the sensor B path
Solder joint that opens under heat or vibration
Electrical interference on the measuring line

symptoms: Warnings that come and go
Brief converter derating
Code stored without a current fault

P0EA0.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit
P0EA0.description: P0EA0 covers circuit faults of a third current channel inside a DC/DC converter, sensor C. Converters with several phases or with separate input and output sensing can carry more than two current channels; the letter C simply names the third. It is used when that reading is missing or cannot be decoded and no sharper diagnosis fits; plausibility, too-low, too-high and unstable signals have P0EA1 to P0EA4. No manufacturer documents P0EA0 or any other sensor C current code in public sources. Ford's hybrid summary describes the kind of current input check involved, where the raw value must stay between 4.5 V and 6.0 V and the offset at power-up under 15 A. Such checks are mandatory under CARB. The equivalent codes for channels A and B are P0E51 and P0E9B.

causes.label: Defect in the converter's third current sensing channel
Damaged connector or wiring on the sensor C path
Software fault in the signal evaluation

symptoms: Warning for the high-voltage or 12 V system
Converter limited to a reduced output
MIL depending on the manufacturer

P0EA1.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0EA1.description: P0EA1 stands for a sensor C current reading that is electrically plausible yet disagrees with the converter's operating point or with its sister channels. If a converter measures several phase currents, those values should track each other, and one channel that deviates is a typical trigger. No manufacturer documents P0EA1 publicly. Ford's P0A94 test illustrates the approach for the boost converter of its hybrids: a deviation of over 50 A between measured and calculated inductor current, held for more than 4 s, counts as a fault. FCA shows how makers adjust such checks, turning the sensor A rationality code P0E52 into a one-trip fault for the Ram 1500 eTorque with flash 08-037-21. Hard circuit faults of sensor C use P0EA0, P0EA2 and P0EA3.

causes.label: Sensor C channel drifting away from the other channels
Fault in the converter phase measured by sensor C
Plausibility software in need of an update

symptoms: MIL, possibly after one trip
Reduced 12 V charging current
Converter or drive power derated

P0EA2.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit Low
P0EA2.description: P0EA2 is stored when current sensor C of a DC/DC converter reports a raw value under its lower limit. Because current sensors in these units normally place their zero-current output at mid-supply, a value near zero volts rarely means low current; it points to a ground short, a lost sensor supply or a broken signal path. No manufacturer documents P0EA2 publicly. The closest published case is Porsche's P0E9D00 on the B channel of the Taycan converter, a short to ground that in fact came from a monitoring threshold set too low and was cured with new software. Ford rates current inputs as faulty below 4.5 V raw. CARB asks for out-of-range checks of such inputs. The high fault of sensor C is P0EA3.

causes.label: Sensor C signal shorted to ground
Missing supply voltage of the current sensor
Monitoring threshold in the software set too tight

symptoms: Warning lamp and possibly a stop request
Converter switched off or derated
12 V battery discharges while driving

P0EA3.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit High
P0EA3.description: P0EA3 marks a current sensor C signal above the top of its accepted window. Electrically this means the signal line touching a voltage source, an open sensor ground or a failed output stage of the sensor; a genuine overcurrent of the converter is a different matter and has its own code, P0D33. No manufacturer documents P0EA3 publicly. Mercedes-Benz illustrates the fault type on the first current channel of the converter in the EQB and the G-Class, which logs P0E5400 for a short to plus; in that bulletin the entry comes from a wrong wake-up of the converter rather than from damaged wiring; a converter reset ends the error state. Ford treats raw current signals above 6.0 V as faulty. If only sensor C is affected, its path is the suspect. The low fault is P0EA2.

causes.label: Sensor C signal shorted to supply
Open ground of the current sensor
Converter error state after wake-up

symptoms: 12 V or high-voltage warning in the cluster
Converter output stopped
Reduced performance possible

P0EA4.title: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0EA4.description: P0EA4 ends the current sensor C series and describes a signal that wavers or breaks off momentarily instead of failing steadily. No manufacturer documents P0EA4 publicly. A comparable published fault exists for the first channel: FCA bulletin 08-333-25 covers P0E55-00, the erratic code of current sensor A, on the 2025 Ram 1500 eTorque V6: there the 12 V battery loses charge, in bad cases until the pickup has to be towed, and FCA answers with a software update of the battery pack controller (BPCM). A software check is therefore worth doing before any part is replaced. CARB obliges makers to supervise such inputs. On the hardware side, a loose plug, a damaged pin or a joint that opens with temperature changes are the usual causes. Steady faults of sensor C are P0EA0, P0EA2 and P0EA3.

causes.label: Outdated control software evaluating the signal too strictly
Loose plug or damaged pin on the sensor C path
Connection that opens with temperature changes

symptoms: Sporadic warnings without a lasting fault
12 V battery not kept fully charged
Start-stop occasionally disabled

P0EA5.title: DC/DC Converter B Performance
P0EA5.description: P0EA5 says that a second DC/DC converter, B, does not deliver what it is asked to, for example the commanded output voltage or current, although its sensors give no circuit fault. FCA documents it as DC/DC Converter 2 Performance for the 2019 Jeep Cherokee (KL) with the 3.2 litre V6 and engine start/stop: PCM flash bulletins 18-023-19 REV. B and 18-077-22 list it with P0EA6 and with communication codes for converter control modules A and B, alongside restart problems after a stop phase. The fix there is new PCM software, done with a charger keeping the battery between 13.2 and 13.5 V. Ford's equivalent test for converter A (P0A94) compares calculated and measured current, 50 A for 4 s. Overheating of converter B is P0EA6.

causes.label: Engine or powertrain control software needing an update
Internal fault of converter B
Poor supply or ground connection of converter B

symptoms: MIL on
Engine does not restart after an auto-stop, start-stop disabled
Voltage dips in the 12 V network, for example audio dropouts

P0EA6.title: DC/DC Converter B Over Temperature
P0EA6.description: P0EA6 means the second DC/DC converter, B, has reached a temperature beyond its permitted limit. Unlike a temperature sensor code, the reading itself is accepted as true; the unit is simply too hot and will normally reduce or stop its output to protect itself. FCA lists it as DC/DC Converter 2 Over Temperature for the 2019 Cherokee (KL) with the 3.2 V6 and stop-start (sales code EHK), in its PCM reflash bulletins (18-077-22, earlier 18-023-19 REV. B), which apply to MIL complaints with a list of start-stop related codes; no threshold is published. Under CARB the function of such parts has to be supervised. Blocked cooling air, high load on the 12 V network or a weak internal power stage are typical causes. Converter A uses P0D32 for the same fault.

causes.label: Cooling air or heat sink of converter B obstructed
Sustained high load on the 12 V network
Control software misjudging the temperature condition
Weak internal power stage of converter B

symptoms: MIL on
Start-stop unavailable while the converter is hot
Electrical consumers affected during engine restart

P0EA7.title: Auxiliary Cooling System Performance
P0EA7.description: P0EA7 reports that an auxiliary cooling loop, a coolant circuit kept apart from the main engine circuit, does not achieve the cooling effect the controller expects. Volvo documents the code for its T8 plug-in hybrids of model years 2016 to 2019 (XC90, S90, XC60, S60 and others): the engine control module stores P0EA773, fault type actuator stuck closed, and turns on the check-engine light. Technical Journal 34123 traces it to the thermostat in the cooling coil of the electric rear axle drive and calls for a revised part with a small orifice, fitted in the correct orientation, followed by a coolant refill. Ford lists P0EA7:19 among codes that faulty dynamics-module software can leave in the PCM of the 2025-2026 Mustang GTD; reprogramming cures it there. Sensor faults of the same loop are P0E81 to P0E84.

causes.label: Thermostat in the auxiliary loop sticking closed (Volvo T8, earlier part design)
Low coolant level or trapped air in the auxiliary loop
Weak or failed auxiliary coolant pump
Module software reporting the fault wrongly (Ford Mustang GTD)

symptoms: Check-engine light on
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Possible power limits on electric drive parts that run too warm

P0EA8.title: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit
P0EA8.description: P0EA8 is the general circuit code for the second high-voltage measurement of an electric A/C compressor, labelled sensor B. Such compressors draw their power from the traction battery and convert it in a built-in inverter; the module reads the supply voltage to control the motor and protect its power stage. Here the B signal is missing or unusable as a whole, without being classed as low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0EA8 publicly, and nobody states which point sensor B measures. For the A channel, GM's 2011 Volt tables show how such inputs are judged (P0D6A at 440 V or more, P0D6B at 190 V or less, each Type B). CARB demands circuit checks on inputs that hybrid battery cooling relies on. Expect the compressor to stop; specific faults are P0EA9 to P0EAC.

causes.label: Interrupted voltage sense path inside or at the compressor
Fault on the compressor's inverter or control board
Poorly seated high-voltage or signal connector at the compressor

symptoms: Air conditioning does not cool
Fault message for the climate system
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be unavailable during charging

P0EA9.title: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit Performance
P0EA9.description: P0EA9 means the B voltage reading reported by the electric A/C compressor looks electrically valid but does not fit other information, usually the high voltage reported by the battery system that feeds the compressor directly. No manufacturer documents P0EA9 publicly. The matching check on sensor A (P0D69) shows typical limits: Mitsubishi's 2019 Outlander PHEV flags a gap of 20 V or more lasting 2 s once the compressor sees 205 to 415 V, the battery is above 15 °C and intake air above 0 °C; GM's 2011 Volt uses more than 15 V in 35 of 40 samples. Mitsubishi names the data bus, the compressor assembly and the hybrid ECU as causes, and a drifting measurement inside the compressor is just as likely for channel B. Hard circuit faults of sensor B are P0EA8, P0EAA and P0EAB.

causes.label: Drifting voltage measurement inside the compressor module
Faulty data exchange between compressor and hybrid controller
Wrong battery voltage reference from the hybrid or battery controller

symptoms: Air conditioning switches off or works only now and then
Fault often recorded without any other symptom

P0EAA.title: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit High
P0EAA.description: P0EAA flags a B voltage reading at the top of, or beyond, the plausible range of the compressor supply. Since the battery cannot really deliver that much, the cause usually lies in the measurement itself: an open or shorted sense path, a failed voltage divider inside the compressor or a wrong reference. No manufacturer documents P0EAA publicly. GM's 2011 Volt judges the A channel this way (P0D6A): 440 V or more in 30 of 60 samples taken every 50 ms, Type B with MIL after two trips; a single sample at 480 V or more triggers a separate maker code. A genuinely high bus voltage would also show up in battery and inverter codes, which helps to tell the two apart. The compressor normally shuts down; the low counterpart is P0EAB.

causes.label: Failed voltage divider or reference in the compressor module
Sense line shorted to a higher potential
Actual overvoltage on the high-voltage bus

symptoms: Compressor stops, cabin is not cooled
Warning in the climate control display

P0EAB.title: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0EAB.description: P0EAB is set when the B voltage channel of the electric A/C compressor reports far less than the high-voltage battery actually supplies while the contactors are closed. Typical reasons are a sense line shorted to ground, a broken internal connection or a sensing stage without supply; a supply interrupted upstream, for instance by a high-voltage fuse, produces the same picture and should be ruled out first. No manufacturer documents P0EAB publicly. For the A channel (P0D6B), GM's 2011 Volt uses 190 V or less in 30 of 60 samples, contactors closed and no faults present, Type B. CARB calls for range checks of such inputs where hybrid cooling depends on them. The air conditioning, and possibly battery cooling, fails; the high counterpart is P0EAA.

causes.label: Voltage sense line shorted to ground
High-voltage supply to the compressor interrupted (fuse, connector)
Measuring stage in the compressor module without supply

symptoms: No cooling from the air conditioning
Charging power may be reduced if the battery cannot be cooled

P0EAC.title: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0EAC.description: P0EAC points to a B voltage signal that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of staying wrong. The module sees sudden changes no real battery voltage can make, or values that come and go. Loose high-voltage or signal connectors at the compressor, vibration damage to the harness, moisture in a plug and internal contact problems on the inverter board are the usual suspects. No manufacturer documents P0EAC publicly; GM and Mitsubishi only publish steady range and plausibility checks for the A channel (P0D6A, P0D6B, P0D69). The fault may vanish after a restart and return with vibration or temperature changes. Wiggle tests are only allowed after the high-voltage circuit is isolated and verified dead. Steady faults of the same sensor are P0EA8 to P0EAB.

causes.label: Loose or corroded connector at the compressor
Harness chafed or cracked by engine and road vibration
Cracked solder joint on the compressor control board

symptoms: Air conditioning cuts out briefly and then resumes
Fault entry returns after clearing

P0EAD.title: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Circuit
P0EAD.description: P0EAD covers the current sensor of an electric A/C compressor, which measures how much current the motor drive takes from the high-voltage link. The controller needs this value to limit power and to shield the power stage and the high-voltage pack from overload. P0EAD is the general circuit code: the reading is absent or useless as a whole, with no low, high or plausibility verdict. Only Audi documents a sibling publicly (P0EAE on the 2016 A3 e-tron); P0EAD itself appears in no manufacturer source. GM's 2011 Volt shows how the measured value is used: above 27 A in 30 of 60 samples while the motor runs gives P0D6F, Type B. Because the sensor sits inside the compressor's power module, repair normally means the compressor assembly. Specific faults are P0EAE to P0EB0.

causes.label: Failed current sensing element in the compressor power module
Open internal connection between sensor and control board
Compressor or climate module software error

symptoms: Compressor does not start, no cooling
Fault stored in the climate or compressor module

P0EAE.title: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Range/Performance
P0EAE.description: P0EAE says the compressor current reading is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state, for example a value that does not match motor speed or load. Audi documents the code for the 2016 A3 e-tron: P0EAE00 is stored as a passive or sporadic entry in the Climatronic module J255, the MIL is lit at the request of another module over the vehicle network while the engine module holds no code, and P26FD00 may appear alongside. Audi bulletin 2047037 blames a software calculation error in the compressor self-test and the refrigerant system check; technicians follow the guided test plan, replace the compressor only if it directs them to, and update J255 from software 0510 to 0520. CARB requires A/C components used by other diagnostics to be monitored. Circuit faults of this sensor are P0EAD, P0EAF and P0EB0.

causes.label: Calculation error in the climate module software (Audi A3 e-tron, update available)
Drifting current measurement in the compressor
Internal compressor fault confirmed by the guided test

symptoms: MIL on without an engine module fault code
Air conditioning may or may not be restricted
Entry stored as passive or sporadic

P0EAF.title: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0EAF.description: P0EAF reports that the compressor current signal sits at the bottom of its measuring range. In a running compressor this cannot be true, so the module suspects the measuring chain: a grounded signal path, a sensing chip without supply or an offset error inside the power module. No manufacturer documents P0EAF publicly. GM's 2011 Volt supervises the measured current only against upper limits (27 A over 30 of 60 samples for P0D6F, 60 A on a single sample for a maker code), and Audi documents only the plausibility sibling P0EAE. Without a valid current value the controller cannot protect the inverter, so it shuts the compressor down. Air conditioning stops working while the car itself remains fully drivable. The high counterpart is P0EB0.

causes.label: Current signal path shorted to ground
Current sensor without supply voltage
Offset error of the measurement in the power module

symptoms: Compressor shut down, warm air from the vents
Climate system fault message

P0EB0.title: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Circuit High
P0EB0.description: P0EB0 flags a current sensor signal at the top end of its range, beyond what the compressor drive could ever draw. It differs from a genuine overcurrent such as P0D6F, where the measurement is trusted and the motor is overloaded: here the signal itself is suspect, for example after a short to a supply voltage or a failed sensing element. No manufacturer documents P0EB0 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt gives a feel for normal limits: more than 27 A over 30 of 60 samples counts as excessive load there, Type B. CARB demands range checks for inputs that hybrid thermal management relies on. If the reading looks plausible after a restart, a stiff compressor or an overfilled refrigerant circuit should still be ruled out. The low counterpart is P0EAF.

causes.label: Current signal shorted to a supply voltage
Failed sensing element in the compressor inverter
Real overload from a stiff compressor or excessive refrigerant charge

symptoms: Compressor switches off right after starting
No cooling, fault message in the climate display

P0EB1.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Circuit
P0EB1.description: Electric A/C compressors run a three-phase permanent-magnet motor whose inverter measures the phase currents in order to commutate it and limit torque. P0EB1 is the general circuit fault of the phase U current sensor: the controller gets no usable signal and gives no finer verdict on it. P0EB1 is not described in any public maker document. GM's 2011 Volt checked the same sensors under the older codes P0D7A to P0D7F, testing at standstill with zero speed request; any reading of 68 A or more in either direction (30 of 60 samples, 50 ms) counted as a sensor fault, Type B, and only a 12 V reset allowed a new pass. The sensor belongs to the inverter, so the usual repair is the compressor assembly. U-phase details: P0EB2 to P0EB4.

causes.label: Failed phase U current sensor in the compressor inverter
Open signal path between sensor and inverter controller
Fault on the inverter control board

symptoms: Compressor does not run, cabin stays warm
Climate system warning

P0EB2.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Circuit High
P0EB2.description: P0EB2 is set when the phase U current sensor of the electric A/C compressor sends a signal above its valid window. Current sensors in such inverters often output a voltage centred on zero current, so a stuck-high output reads like a large current in one direction even with the motor at rest. No manufacturer documents P0EB2 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt ran a standstill test that catches exactly this: plus 68 A or more on phase U with no speed request set the older code P0D7A, Type B. A short to the sensor supply, a damaged Hall element or a fault on the inverter board are typical. The compressor controller stops the motor to protect the power stage. P0EB3 covers the low side; P0EB5 and P0EB8 report the same fault on phases V and W.

causes.label: Phase U signal shorted to the sensor supply
Damaged Hall element of the phase U sensor
Defect on the inverter board affecting the U channel

symptoms: Compressor will not start or stops at once
No cooling during hot weather

P0EB3.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0EB3.description: P0EB3 means the phase U current signal has fallen below its permitted range. Depending on the sensor design this looks like a large negative current or like no signal at all; either way the controller can no longer trust the U-phase value it needs to drive the motor smoothly. No maker documents P0EB3 publicly. In GM's 2011 Volt, a phase U reading of minus 68 A or lower with the compressor at rest set the older code P0D7B, Type B with MIL after two trips, and a 12 V reset was needed before the test could pass again. Likely causes are a ground short in the sensing path, lost sensor supply or an internal inverter fault. Cooling stays off until the fault clears. Counterpart: P0EB2; the same fault on V and W: P0EB6, P0EB9.

causes.label: Phase U sensing path shorted to ground
Supply to the phase U sensor missing
Internal fault in the compressor inverter

symptoms: Air conditioning inoperative
Fault message after switching the A/C on

P0EB4.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Range/Performance
P0EB4.description: P0EB4 concerns the plausibility of the phase U current reading of an electric A/C compressor. The value is in range but disagrees with what the controller can work out for itself: in a motor fed by three wires the phase currents must add up to roughly zero, and each phase should follow the commanded current pattern. A standing offset or a wrong gain while running are typical findings. No manufacturer documents P0EB4 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt looked for offsets on its compressor phases only with the motor stopped (plus or minus 68 A, older codes P0D7A and P0D7B). A weakening sensor element or inverter board is the usual cause, so the compressor assembly gets replaced. Electrical faults of phase U are P0EB1 to P0EB3.

causes.label: Offset or gain drift of the phase U sensor
Ageing measurement circuit on the inverter board
Winding fault in the compressor motor distorting the currents

symptoms: Compressor runs roughly or noisily before switching off
Reduced or intermittent cooling

P0EB5.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Circuit High
P0EB5.description: P0EB5 is the high-range fault of the phase V current sensor in the compressor inverter. The reading lies above the window the sensor can produce in normal service, which points to a short towards supply voltage, a defective sensing element or an internal fault in the power module rather than to real overcurrent. Unusually, the V-phase codes start with high, low and plausibility, while the general V circuit code comes later as P0EBB. No manufacturer documents P0EB5 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt detected a stuck V-phase sensor at standstill at plus 68 A or more under the older code P0D7C, Type B. The compressor drive is switched off, and refrigerant-based battery cooling may be lost with it. Related codes: P0EB6, P0EB7 and P0EBB.

causes.label: Phase V signal shorted towards supply voltage
Defective phase V sensing element
Internal fault in the compressor power module

symptoms: Compressor switched off, no cooling
Battery may warm up more during fast charging

P0EB6.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0EB6.description: P0EB6 reports that the phase V current signal reads below its permissible minimum. The compressor's power module cannot regulate phase V without it and stops the motor. Candidates are a sensing path pulled to ground, a sensor that has lost its supply or a defect on the inverter board; a problem in the refrigerant circuit cannot produce this code. No manufacturer documents P0EB6 publicly. In the first-generation Chevrolet Volt, GM treated minus 68 A or lower on phase V with the motor at rest as a sensor fault (older code P0D7D, 30 of 60 samples, Type B). Because the sensor is built in, replacing the compressor unit is the normal fix. High range: P0EB5; general V circuit: P0EBB; the phase U and W equivalents are P0EB3 and P0EB9.

causes.label: Phase V sensing path pulled to ground
Phase V sensor has lost its supply
Defect in the V channel of the inverter board

symptoms: No air conditioning
Fault stored in the compressor control module

P0EB7.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Range/Performance
P0EB7.description: With P0EB7 the compressor's phase V current value passes the electrical limits but is not credible. The controller compares it with the other two phases and with the current it is commanding; a persistent offset, a reading that lags or is scaled wrongly, or a three-phase sum far from zero all point at the V sensor. No manufacturer documents P0EB7 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt shows one form of such a check, performed at standstill (older codes P0D7C and P0D7D at plus or minus 68 A). Rough compressor running, noise or reduced cooling can appear before the controller gives up and switches off. Electrical faults of the same phase are P0EB5, P0EB6 and P0EBB; the matching checks on U and W are P0EB4 and P0EBA.

causes.label: Persistent offset or scaling error of the phase V sensor
Slow or filtered V-phase measurement on the inverter board
Fault in the V winding or its internal lead

symptoms: Uneven compressor running or humming noise
Cooling weakens, then fails

P0EB8.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Circuit High
P0EB8.description: P0EB8 indicates that the phase W current sensor of the compressor inverter delivers a value above its usable range. Since the motor is not actually drawing such a current, a short to a positive supply in the sensing circuit or a failed sensor element is the most probable explanation. The W-phase series runs high, low and plausibility from P0EB8 to P0EBA, while the general W circuit code sits apart at P0EC0. No manufacturer documents P0EB8 publicly. GM's first-generation Volt flagged a W-phase reading of plus 68 A or more with the motor stopped under the older code P0D7E, Type B, and demanded a 12 V reset before the test could pass. Air conditioning stops. Counterpart: P0EB9; the same fault on U and V: P0EB2, P0EB5.

causes.label: W-phase sensing circuit shorted to a positive supply
Failed phase W sensor element
Fault in the W input of the inverter controller

symptoms: A/C stops working, warning shown
Compressor will not restart until the fault is cleared

P0EB9.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0EB9.description: P0EB9 is stored when the phase W current signal drops beneath its lower limit, for instance after the signal wire has made contact with ground or after the sensor has lost its feed. The value is then useless for motor control, and the compressor module shuts the drive down rather than run it on two phases of information. No manufacturer documents P0EB9 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt shows a comparable test: minus 68 A or lower on phase W at standstill set the older code P0D7F, rated Type B with MIL after two trips. Because the sensing sits inside the compressor, repair usually means replacing the compressor assembly once wiring and high-voltage plugs have been checked. High range: P0EB8; plausibility: P0EBA; general W circuit: P0EC0.

causes.label: Phase W measuring line shorted to ground
Phase W sensor without supply
Defect of the W measurement inside the compressor module

symptoms: No cooling, compressor silent
Climate fault indicated

P0EBA.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Range/Performance
P0EBA.description: P0EBA covers an implausible phase W current reading in an electric A/C compressor: the signal stays in range, yet it does not agree with the commanded current, the rotor position or the two other phases. No manufacturer documents P0EBA publicly. GM's 2011 Volt used a standstill check for sensor offsets on phase W, filed under the older codes P0D7E and P0D7F at plus or minus 68 A, 30 of 60 samples, Type B. In practice an ageing current sensor or a fault on the inverter board is behind it, and since both live inside the compressor, the assembly is replaced after the high-voltage system has been made safe and the connectors have been inspected. The compressor may run unevenly before the controller cuts it out. Electrical faults of phase W: P0EB8, P0EB9 and P0EC0.

causes.label: Ageing phase W current sensor
Fault in the W measurement on the inverter board
Rotor position estimate disturbed, making the W current look wrong

symptoms: Compressor runs unevenly, then stops
Cooling capacity drops

P0EBB.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Circuit
P0EBB.description: P0EBB is the general circuit code for the compressor's phase V current sensor, numbered after the W-phase codes instead of at the start of the V series. The module receives no usable V-phase value at all and does not classify it further as high, low or implausible. Without that value the field-oriented control of the three-phase motor cannot work, so the drive stops. No manufacturer documents P0EBB publicly. GM's 2011 Volt monitored the phase sensors of its compressor at standstill under older codes (P0D7C and P0D7D for phase V, plus or minus 68 A, Type B). Causes are an open sensing path, a loose internal plug or a failed sensor or board. Detailed V-phase faults are P0EB5 to P0EB7; the general U and W circuit codes are P0EB1 and P0EC0.

causes.label: Open phase V sensing path
Loose internal plug between sensor and board
Failed phase V sensor or inverter board

symptoms: Compressor does not run
Air conditioning and possibly battery cooling unavailable

P0EBC.title: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0EBC.description: P0EBC is the general circuit fault of the first refrigerant temperature sensor in the air conditioning loop: the control module gets no usable reading from it and does not narrow the fault down to high or low. Volkswagen lists P0EBC00 for the 2021 ID.4 as an electrical fault of refrigerant temperature sensor 1 in the A/C module (address 0008). There the value comes from G395, a combined pressure and temperature sender on the low-pressure line, and bulletin 87-22-01 cures it by replacing that sender, which means draining and recharging the refrigerant. The A/C may stop cooling. Voltage faults of the same sensor are P0EBD and P0EBE, plausibility is P0EBF.

causes.label: Internal electrical fault of the refrigerant pressure/temperature sender (VW G395)
Corroded connector or damaged wiring to the sensor
Faulty sensor input in the climate control module

symptoms: Air conditioning inoperative or not cooling
Fault entry stored in the climate control module

P0EBD.title: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0EBD.description: P0EBD means the signal voltage of refrigerant temperature sensor A sits at the top of its range. With the usual NTC thermistor that equals an extremely cold reading, and in practice it points to an open signal path, a disconnected plug or a short to the reference voltage. No manufacturer documents P0EBD publicly. As a comparison for the same kind of sensor, GM's 2012 Volt flags its evaporator refrigerant sensor above 98 percent of the 5 V reference (about 4.9 V) in 40 of 50 samples, Type B, under P0538. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV treats a high input lasting 4 seconds as an open circuit. A wrong cold value can block compressor operation. The low-voltage counterpart is P0EBE.

causes.label: Open signal or ground wire, or unplugged connector
Thermistor open internally
Signal wire shorted to the reference or supply voltage

symptoms: Compressor stays off or A/C output is reduced
Implausibly low refrigerant temperature in live data

P0EBE.title: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0EBE.description: P0EBE is logged when the voltage from refrigerant temperature sensor A falls close to zero. For an NTC element a low voltage stands for high temperature, so the controller sees refrigerant that seems far too hot. Real heat at that level is unlikely; a signal wire chafed through to ground or a thermistor shorted internally is the usual finding. No manufacturer publishes P0EBE. GM's 2012 Volt reacts to its evaporator refrigerant sensor below 2 percent of the reference (about 0.1 V) in 40 of 50 samples as P0537, Type B, which shows how such a check is built. Expect the compressor to be held off as protection. High-voltage fault of this sensor: P0EBD.

causes.label: Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Thermistor shorted internally
Moisture bridging the connector pins

symptoms: A/C compressor switched off as a precaution
Live data shows an unrealistically hot refrigerant

P0EBF.title: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
P0EBF.description: P0EBF reports that sensor A gives an electrically valid but implausible refrigerant temperature. Three makers name it. Audi stores P0EBF00 as passive or sporadic in the Climatronic module of the 2016 A3 e-tron; bulletin 2047037 blames a miscalculation in the refrigerant self-check and points to TSB 2046942. VW's 2021 ID.4 links it to the G395 sender, which is replaced. Volvo logs P0EBF24 in the engine module of its 2017 to 2019 S90, V60, XC60 and XC90, lighting the check engine lamp: when the car had been pre-heated or pre-cooled, or started remotely, while the traction battery was charged, the software misjudged the sensor, and Technical Journal 34446 ends with a software update. Circuit faults are P0EBC to P0EBE.

causes.label: Software misjudgement after preconditioning or self-check (Volvo, Audi; update available)
Deviating pressure/temperature sender (VW G395)
Wrong refrigerant charge distorting the comparison values

symptoms: Check engine lamp on (Volvo) or MIL requested by the climate module (Audi)
Fault stored as intermittent or sporadic
A/C may cool poorly or not at all

P0EC0.title: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Circuit
P0EC0.description: P0EC0 is the umbrella circuit code for the phase W current sensor in the inverter of an electric A/C compressor. It applies when no valid W-phase value arrives at all, without a split into high, low or implausible; those cases have their own codes P0EB8 to P0EBA. Like the phase V circuit code P0EBB it is numbered out of sequence. No manufacturer documents P0EC0 publicly. For orientation, GM's 2011 Volt checked each compressor phase with the motor stopped and set a fault when the W reading stayed beyond plus or minus 68 A in 30 of 60 samples (older codes P0D7E and P0D7F, Type B, 12 V reset needed). Without the W value the motor control cannot run the compressor. U-phase circuit code: P0EB1.

causes.label: Interrupted W-phase sensing path inside the inverter
Failed W-phase current sensor or inverter board
Missing supply voltage for the current sensors

symptoms: Electric A/C compressor does not start
No cabin cooling, battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited

P0EC1.title: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0EC1.description: P0EC1 covers a circuit fault of a second refrigerant temperature sensor, found mainly on electrified cars whose heat pump or battery chiller measures the refrigerant at several points. The module receives no usable value from sensor B. No manufacturer publishes P0EC1 or says which of its sensors counts as B. Volkswagen's e-Golf shows how such networks look: up to five combined pressure/temperature senders (G395, G826 to G829) share two LIN lines, and because early parts could not be auto-addressed, bulletin 87-17-02 requires replacing every sender on the affected line. Without B the heat pump or A/C may shut down. Detailed faults of sensor B: P0EC2 to P0EC4; sensor A: P0EBC.

causes.label: Failed sensor B or combined pressure/temperature sender
Wiring, connector or shared LIN line fault
Mixed part versions on one LIN line after a repair

symptoms: Heat pump or A/C switched off or limited
Fault stored in the climate control module

P0EC2.title: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0EC2.description: With P0EC2 the signal of refrigerant temperature sensor B is stuck near the reference voltage. An NTC thermistor would only get there at extreme cold, so an open circuit somewhere in the loop is far more likely. No manufacturer documents P0EC2 publicly. Mitsubishi's procedure for the analogous evaporator outlet sensor of the Outlander PHEV shows the logic: the A/C amplifier sets its open-circuit code after 4 seconds of high input while READY is on or the battery is charging, and the technician measures about 5 V at the unplugged connector and checks both lines for continuity under 2 ohms. A false cold reading may lock out heating or cooling. Low counterpart: P0EC3.

causes.label: Open signal or ground line between sensor B and module
Connector not fully seated after A/C work
Sensor B open internally

symptoms: Very low refrigerant temperature shown for sensor B
Heating via heat pump or cooling unavailable

P0EC3.title: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0EC3.description: P0EC3 stands for a sensor B signal pulled down toward ground. Because a thermistor of the NTC type lowers its resistance as it warms, the module reads a refrigerant temperature far above anything the system could reach. Typical culprits are a harness pinched against the body, water inside the plug or a sensor that has failed shorted. P0EC3 appears in no public manufacturer document. GM's evaporator sensor check on the 2012 Volt (P0537, below roughly 0.1 V, two trips) is the nearest documented model. On cars that cool the traction battery through the refrigerant loop the controller may restrict that cooling as well as the cabin A/C. Open-circuit side: P0EC2; sensor A equivalent: P0EBE.

causes.label: Harness pinched against the body, signal shorted to ground
Water ingress in the sensor plug
Sensor B shorted internally

symptoms: A/C compressor held off, cabin not cooled
Charging or driving power possibly limited if battery cooling depends on the loop

P0EC4.title: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance
P0EC4.description: P0EC4 is a plausibility fault: sensor B delivers a voltage inside its normal window, yet the temperature it reports does not agree with other information. No manufacturer documents P0EC4 publicly. A well-described pattern comes from GM's 2012 Volt (P153B, Type B): once the compressor has been off for over an hour, the low-side refrigerant temperature must lie within 10 degrees Celsius of the raw ambient temperature and of the value derived from high-side pressure; the check runs only when no circuit codes are active. A drifting sensor, poor thermal contact or a wrong charge can fail such a comparison. The A/C usually still works but may be controlled poorly. Electrical faults of sensor B: P0EC1 to P0EC3.

causes.label: Sensor B drifting out of tolerance
Sensor not seated properly on the pipe, poor thermal contact
Incorrect refrigerant charge shifting the comparison values

symptoms: Uneven or weak cooling, compressor cycling oddly
Fault often appears only after a long standstill

P0EC5.title: A/C Compressor Motor Speed Sensor Range/Performance
P0EC5.description: P0EC5 means the speed information of the electrically driven compressor motor is implausible: the motor does not turn at the speed the controller expects, or the reported value contradicts other data. Mazda uses the code on the 2024 to 2026 CX-90 PHEV and 2025 to 2026 CX-70 PHEV, describing P0EC5:00 in the PCM as an error signal coming from the compressor. Bulletin 07-002/26b lists it beside P0D6D, U0605 and P0AA6 when an overcurrent shorts the compressor internally and the high-voltage A/C fuse blows; the A/C then stops cooling. GM's 2011 Volt ran a similar test as P1F0A, Type B: fault if the spinning motor stays below 1800 rpm for 20 seconds.

causes.label: Internal short in the electric compressor after overcurrent (Mazda PHEV)
Blown high-voltage A/C fuse cutting compressor power
Mechanical drag or lack of oil keeping the motor below target speed

symptoms: A/C does not cool
Accompanying compressor voltage, communication or insulation codes

P0EC6.title: A/C Power Supply Relay Control Circuit/Open
P0EC6.description: P0EC6 concerns the control side of the relay that switches power to air conditioning components, typically the compressor or climate electronics. The module driving the relay coil notices that its output does not behave as commanded, most often because the coil circuit is open. No manufacturer documents P0EC6 publicly, and the exact wiring differs by maker. CARB requires output components to be checked either functionally or for circuit continuity and shorts, and lets manufacturers report open and shorted states under one code, which is the role of this umbrella code. A relay that never pulls in leaves the A/C without power. Voltage-specific faults: P0EC7 and P0EC8; the clutch relay equivalent is P0645.

causes.label: Relay coil burnt open or relay missing
Open control wire or loose relay socket terminal
Failed output driver in the controlling module

symptoms: A/C or electric compressor completely without function
No relay click when A/C is requested

P0EC7.title: A/C Power Supply Relay Control Circuit Low
P0EC7.description: P0EC7 is set when the control line of the relay feeding the A/C reads too low a voltage, usually because it is shorted to ground. What the driver feels depends on how the coil is switched: with a low-side driver a grounded line can keep the relay energised even with the A/C off, while with a high-side driver the relay simply cannot be switched on. No manufacturer documents P0EC7 publicly. As a comparison, Mitsubishi monitors a relay-fed supply on its throttle actuator (P0657): with battery voltage above 8.3 V, the switched line must not sit at or below 6.0 V for 0.35 seconds. Open-circuit code: P0EC6; high counterpart: P0EC8; clutch relay analogue: P0646.

causes.label: Relay control line chafed and shorted to ground
Shorted turns in the relay coil
Output stage of the module stuck low

symptoms: A/C power stays on with A/C switched off, or never switches on
Possible battery drain while parked if the relay stays energised

P0EC8.title: A/C Power Supply Relay Control Circuit High
P0EC8.description: P0EC8 indicates that the relay control circuit for the A/C power supply carries too high a voltage, typically a short to a battery-fed wire. A low-side driver then pushes current straight into that short when it switches on; modern output stages detect the overcurrent, turn themselves off and log this code, so the relay stays open and the A/C components get no power. With a high-side driver the same fault can hold the relay on permanently. No manufacturer documents P0EC8 publicly. CARB explicitly lists shorts toward a higher voltage as a circuit fault that output component monitoring must catch. Look for wires rubbing on a powered conductor or a shorted coil. Low side: P0EC7; clutch relay analogue: P0647.

causes.label: Control line shorted to a battery-fed wire
Relay coil with too low resistance overloading the driver
Incorrect relay type fitted

symptoms: A/C has no power and stays off
Relay may stay energised permanently on high-side switched designs

P0EC9.title: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Stuck/Open
P0EC9.description: P0EC9 reports that refrigerant distribution valve A, a solenoid valve that splits refrigerant between branches of the A/C circuit, stays open or does not close on command. Such a fault is usually detected indirectly, because pressure or temperature behind the valve fails to react when it should be shut. Audi uses the code on the 2016 A3 Sportback e-tron: P0EC900 is logged passive/sporadic in the Climatronic module J255, and the MIL is switched on at the request of another module over the network, so the engine module J623 holds no code. Bulletins 2046942 and 2047037 trace it to a miscalculation in the refrigerant self-test and call for new J255 software; if the code returns after erasing, it has to be diagnosed as a real fault. Circuit faults of valve A are P2611 to P2613, valve B stuck open is P0EE2.

causes.label: Faulty self-test calculation in the climate control software (Audi A3 e-tron, fixed by update)
Valve held open by dirt, debris or a sticking armature
Weak solenoid coil that no longer pulls the valve fully shut

symptoms: MIL on without a code in the engine control module
Code stored passive/sporadic in the climate control module
Reduced or uneven cooling in one branch, or no noticeable change at all

P0ECA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor System - Multiple Sensor Correlation
P0ECA.description: P0ECA treats the temperature sensors of the hybrid or traction battery as one system: the battery controller compares the readings with each other and flags the group when one of them strays from the rest or shows an impossible value. Ford documents it for its 2019 hybrid and plug-in models. The BECM runs the check all the time and sets P0ECA after three or more 5-second events in which a thermistor deviates from the average by more than 25 °C, reads above 95 °C or reads below −50 °C. Bentley stores P0ECA00 in address 0021, the 48 V super capacitor of the Bentayga's Dynamic Ride, alongside P0A9E and P0AC8; the cure is software version 114, after which the part number ends in F. GM files comparable checks under single-sensor codes such as P0A9C instead. Battery power is reduced.

causes.label: One battery thermistor drifting away from the others
Battery controller software misjudging the comparison (Bentley super capacitor, update 114)
Loose or corroded connector on the temperature sense harness inside the pack
Genuine local hot spot, e.g. a blocked cooling channel at one module

symptoms: Hybrid or battery warning, MIL depending on manufacturer
Reduced electric power or charging rate
On the Bentayga, Dynamic Ride fault message and no roll compensation

P0ECB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sensor System - Multiple Sensor Correlation
P0ECB.description: P0ECB indicates that the voltage measurements of the hybrid/EV battery contradict each other. Battery controllers usually capture the same voltage along more than one path, for example the whole pack directly and as the sum of all cell readings, or each half of the pack against its own cells; once these paths drift apart, at least one sensor must be wrong. No manufacturer documents P0ECB publicly. GM runs exactly this comparison under P0ABB: a gap of more than 12 V between pack voltage and cell sum in 20 of 25 samples is a Type A fault. Ford checks each half pack against the total of its cells and fails above 42 V on plug-in and 38 V on full hybrids held for one second (P0B15, P0B1A). Since state of charge is no longer reliable, power is limited.

causes.label: Drifting pack or half-pack voltage sensor in the battery controller
Loose or corroded cell sense lead falsifying the cell sum
Internal fault of the cell monitoring electronics
Measurement taken on the wrong side of a contactor that is not fully closed

symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning
Limited electric power, unstable state of charge display
Contactors may stay open, vehicle may not reach ready mode

P0ECC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery E Voltage
P0ECC.description: P0ECC is the general voltage code for hybrid/EV battery E. The letters A to F mark separately monitored sub-batteries, modules or energy stores of one system; E is the fifth, so the code can only occur where a manufacturer divides its storage into at least five such units. It signals a voltage of this unit that does not fit expectation, without saying whether it fluctuates (P0ECD), sits too low (P0ECE) or too high (P0ECF). No manufacturer documents P0ECC publicly. CARB asks for monitoring of the cells and voltage sensors of hybrid storage with codes that name the smallest replaceable unit, which explains such letter series. As a pack-level reference, GM's P0ABB compares pack voltage with the cell sum at a 12 V limit. The driver sees a battery warning.

causes.label: Aged or damaged cells in unit E
Fault in the voltage sense leads or connectors of unit E
Battery controller measuring or software fault

symptoms: Battery or hybrid warning, MIL
Reduced electric power and range

P0ECD.title: Hybrid/EV Battery E Voltage Unstable
P0ECD.description: P0ECD flags an unstable voltage in hybrid/EV battery E: the value moves faster or further than the controller tolerates, whereas a lasting offset would set P0ECE or P0ECF. No manufacturer documents P0ECD publicly. How such a test can look is shown by Ford for battery A (P0B24) on its 2019 hybrids: the BECM watches continuously and fails the unit once any cell stays more than 0.5 V off the mean of all cells for 15 seconds. Applied to unit E, a weak cell sagging under load, a loose busbar screw or a corroded sense terminal create the same pattern. As these causes depend on load and vibration, the warning may show up while driving and disappear at rest. The general code of the unit is P0ECC; the same fault on unit F is P0ED1.

causes.label: Cell with high internal resistance whose voltage collapses under load
Loose busbar screw or cell connector in unit E
Corroded or intermittent voltage sense terminal
Battery controller software, curable by update

symptoms: Intermittent battery warning, often only under load
Power drops during acceleration
MIL on

P0ECE.title: Hybrid/EV Battery E Voltage Low
P0ECE.description: P0ECE sets when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery E remains below the window the controller expects for the present load and charge. Its counterparts are P0ECF for too high and P0ECD for unstable readings. No manufacturer documents P0ECE publicly. Ford publishes a comparable low test for battery A (P0B25) on its 2019 hybrids, based on calculated state of charge: if any cell reaches 0 % for 10 seconds with the main contactors closed, or for 90 seconds with them open, the code is set. A unit that discharged itself during long standstill, a module with an internal short, or a balancing circuit that keeps draining one group can pull unit E down. The controller then reduces discharge power, so electric range and boost shrink and the engine runs more often on hybrids.

causes.label: Unit E deeply discharged after long standstill or a high self-discharge cell
Internal short or capacity loss in a module of unit E
Balancing switch stuck on and draining one cell group
Voltage sense fault reading low

symptoms: Reduced electric range and acceleration
Engine starts more often, EV mode unavailable
MIL and battery warning

P0ECF.title: Hybrid/EV Battery E Voltage High
P0ECF.description: P0ECF is stored when unit E of the hybrid/EV battery exceeds its upper voltage limit. It mirrors P0ECE, while unstable readings belong to P0ECD. No manufacturer documents P0ECF publicly. Ford's overcharge logic for its 2019 hybrids gives a sense of the limits involved: with the charge contactors open, a cell above 4.5 V on plug-in models or 4.35 V on full hybrids for 2 or 3 seconds counts as a fault under the state-of-charge code P0C30. Overvoltage in one unit typically follows broken cell balancing, a fault in charge or regeneration control, or a measuring channel that reads high. Because overcharged lithium cells are a safety risk, the controller blocks charging and regenerative braking and may open the contactors. Plug-in charging may be refused.

causes.label: Cell balancing of unit E no longer works, group overcharged
Charge or regeneration control error
Voltage sense channel reading too high

symptoms: Charging or regenerative braking blocked
Battery warning, MIL
Vehicle may switch off the high-voltage system

P0ED0.title: Hybrid/EV Battery F Voltage
P0ED0.description: P0ED0 is the general voltage code of hybrid/EV battery F, the sixth and last unit in this letter series. It reports an implausible voltage of the unit without separating unstable (P0ED1), low (P0ED2) and high (P0ED3) readings. Only storage systems divided into six or more separately monitored units can produce it, and no manufacturer documents P0ED0 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid BECM is an example of finely divided monitoring: it supervises the cells in groups of six per sense circuit and fails a circuit when any cell reads above 5 V or below 1 V for 11 seconds. CARB demands that the cells and voltage sensors of the energy storage are monitored with codes for the smallest replaceable unit. A battery warning and reduced power follow.

causes.label: Aged or damaged cells in unit F
Open or high-resistance voltage sense lead of unit F
Cell monitoring electronics or software fault

symptoms: MIL and battery warning
Reduced electric power

P0ED1.title: Hybrid/EV Battery F Voltage Unstable
P0ED1.description: P0ED1 reports that the voltage of hybrid/EV battery F fluctuates beyond the permitted band instead of staying steadily off, which would be P0ED2 or P0ED3. No manufacturer documents P0ED1 publicly. CARB not only requires every cell and voltage sensor of the storage to be watched, it also asks for proof that cell balancing can hold each cell at its intended voltage, and an unsteady unit voltage is often the first hint that a cell group is running away from the others. Ford's comparable test for battery A uses a 0.5 V spread between one cell and the average, held for 15 seconds. Mechanical causes such as a loose busbar or a sense lead with poor contact make the reading jump with vibration. General code of unit F: P0ED0; the same fault on unit E: P0ECD.

causes.label: Cell group of unit F drifting because balancing cannot keep up
Loose busbar or cell connector
Sense lead or connector with intermittent contact

symptoms: Warning that comes and goes, often over bumps or under load
Short power reductions while driving
MIL on

P0ED2.title: Hybrid/EV Battery F Voltage Low
P0ED2.description: P0ED2 means hybrid/EV battery F delivers less voltage than the controller predicts from current draw and state of charge. No manufacturer documents P0ED2 publicly. Published undervoltage limits exist for whole packs: GM's hybrid tables fail the pack below 24 V (P0ABC), and Ford sets P0A7D during cranking if its pack reads under 184.8 V on plug-in or 167.2 V on full hybrids, or if the weakest cell drops below 2.1 V for half a second. For one unit the limits scale with its number of cells. Typical causes are an aged module with lost capacity, a cell with internal leakage that drained during standstill, or a high-resistance joint that loses voltage under load. Discharge power is cut back. High voltage of unit F is P0ED3, low voltage of unit E is P0ECE.

causes.label: Aged module in unit F with lost capacity
Cell with internal leakage drained during standstill
High-resistance connection inside unit F dropping voltage under load

symptoms: Less power in electric mode
Shorter electric range
MIL and battery warning

P0ED3.title: Hybrid/EV Battery F Voltage High
P0ED3.description: P0ED3 is logged once battery F of the hybrid/EV system climbs above its permitted maximum voltage. It is the high member of the F series, next to P0ED2 (low) and P0ED1 (unstable). No manufacturer documents P0ED3 publicly. GM's hybrid tables show how strictly overvoltage is treated at pack level: above 479 V the P0ABD monitor fails within one trip. Ford sets P0AFB when its pack stays above 362.2 V on plug-in or 327.8 V on full hybrids for 10 seconds. Within a single unit an excess voltage usually means its cells were charged further than the rest, for instance because the balancing circuit of that unit quit, or that its measuring channel reads high. Charging and regeneration stay restricted until the cause is found; a warning appears and plug-in charging may be refused.
